Does Florida use a transfer on death deed?

Florida homeowners who want a house to skip probate generally use an enhanced life estate deed, commonly called a lady bird deed. Before using any form labeled a TOD deed that you find online, ask a Florida real property attorney whether the statutes authorize it.

The practical goal is the same either way: the owner keeps control during life and the house passes to named people at death. Below is the lady bird version, the homestead rule that limits it and the tax and title points a buyer or heir will meet.

How a lady bird deed works

The owner keeps a life estate with extra powers, and the remainder passes to named beneficiaries. During life the owner may sell, lease or otherwise transfer the property without the remainder persons' consent. If there is no sale, title passes to them at death once a death certificate is filed in the official records.

Florida attorneys who use these deeds report that one costs about the same as a simple will, and that it suits families whose main asset is the home and whose heirs could not easily pay for a probate.

Is a lady bird deed subject to documentary stamp tax?

On the facts reviewed in one Department of Revenue advisement, no. Technical Assistance Advisement 20B4-004, dated October 16, 2020, found that the deed in question did not transfer any present beneficial interest, so it was not subject to documentary stamp tax whatever consideration was stated. The life tenants in that case kept full powers.

An advisement answers a specific set of facts, so a family should confirm treatment with the clerk's office or the attorney drafting the deed. The general rule points the other way: quit claim and life estate deeds are taxable, and there is no specific exemption for estate planning transfers of Florida real property.

Why homestead complicates a deed at death

Florida limits what an owner can leave by will or trust. Homestead cannot be devised when the owner leaves a spouse or a minor child, except that it may go to a spouse if there is no minor child.

A trust disposition counts as a devise. So owners with a spouse or young children should speak to an attorney about whether the deed they plan will work as intended. A deed signed years earlier can behave differently from a will, and the attorney's answer depends on the family and the property.

Property taxes after a transfer of title

A change of ownership usually resets assessed value to just value the following January 1. Any sale, foreclosure or transfer of legal or beneficial title counts, with exceptions such as transfers between spouses and certain transfers at death.

  • A quitclaim is a change of ownership unless an exception applies, such as the same person remaining entitled, a spouse transfer or a correction.
  • Homestead status requires the owner's permanent residence and an application by March 1.
  • Heirs who do not live in the house do not qualify for homestead on it.

Ask the county property appraiser how a particular deed will affect next year's assessment.

Signing and recording rules for a Florida deed

A conveyance of an interest in land needs a signed writing made in front of two subscribing witnesses. No seal is needed, and witnessing can happen by audio-video technology.

Recording takes place at the clerk's office. The recording charge is five dollars for page one and four dollars for each extra page, with a trust fund charge and a technology charge per page on top. Call the recording desk for the total on your deed, because page count drives it.

When an heir wants to sell

After the owner dies, the beneficiaries hold the property, and the title insurer will want to see the recorded instrument and a death certificate. Sometimes it asks for additional proof on liens or the owner's marital status.

Ways to pass a house at death
ToolMain point
Lady bird deedOwner keeps power to sell; passes at death
Will or trustHomestead limits for spouse and minor children
Quitclaim deedTaxable deed; change of ownership unless exception

Heirs planning a sale should check early that every beneficiary will sign the sale deed. A cash buyer who takes the house as it stands can close quickly once the recorded deed and death certificate are in order.

Risks of a lady bird deed

The main risk is a gap between the family's plan and the facts. A deed may name beneficiaries who die first, and a beneficiary's own creditors or divorce may touch what that person is due to receive. The attorney should address each before recording.

Another risk is paper that sits unrecorded. A deed that never reaches the Official Records gives a buyer or a title insurer nothing to read. Title passes at death by filing a death certificate in the official records, so the recording step carries real weight.

Families also forget that the deed controls only that house. Bank accounts, vehicles and other assets need their own beneficiary designations, and a will still matters for anything outside the deed. Pair the deed with pay on death and beneficiary designations on financial accounts.

Questions for your attorney before signing

Bring a list, because the deed has effects beyond probate.

  • Does the deed fit my homestead situation if I have a spouse or minor child?
  • Will recording it reset the assessed value or affect my exemptions?
  • Which of my children or relatives will need to sign if I sell during my life?
  • What happens if a beneficiary dies before me, or if I want to change my mind?
  • Does my mortgage lender or title insurer need notice?

You keep the power to sell or transfer the property without the remainder persons' consent, which is the feature most families want. The attorney can also tell you how a deed interacts with a will already on file and with beneficiary designations on bank accounts.

Families sometimes find an old deed in a drawer and wonder whether it already did the job. Read the recorded version at the clerk's office, not a copy, since the recorded text controls.

A sensible order of steps

Start with the family facts: who is married, who has minor children, and whether any beneficiary could die first or run into creditors or a divorce. Take those facts and the existing will, mortgage papers and bank beneficiary forms to a Florida real property attorney. Once the deed is drafted, have it signed before two subscribing witnesses, record it with the clerk, and keep the recorded copy with your other papers.

At the owner's death the beneficiaries file the death certificate in the official records. If they plan to sell, they then give the title company the recorded deed, the death certificate and any proof it asks for on liens or marital status, and confirm every beneficiary will sign the sale deed.

Frequently asked questions

Is a TOD deed available to Florida owners?

Ask a Florida real property attorney. Florida owners commonly use an enhanced life estate deed, also called a lady bird deed, to pass a house at death.

Does a lady bird deed avoid probate?

It is designed to, by passing title to the beneficiaries at death once a death certificate is recorded. Your attorney can confirm that it fits your family and your homestead situation.

Does a lady bird deed pay doc stamp tax?

One 2020 advisement found no tax on the facts presented, because no present beneficial interest passed. Confirm your own deed with the clerk or attorney.

Can homestead be left to anyone?

No. With a surviving spouse or minor child, homestead cannot be devised, except to the spouse when there is no minor child.

How many witnesses does a Florida deed need?

Two subscribing witnesses, and no seal. Witnessing can use audio-video technology.

Florida Lady Bird Deed: Enhanced Life Estate Deeds and Selling the Home

A Florida enhanced life estate deed, usually called a lady bird deed, lets the grantor keep a life estate and control of the property while naming who receives it later. This guide uses a clerk-published form and the Florida Constitution's homestead rules.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

What a lady bird deed is

A lady bird deed, also called an enhanced life estate deed, leaves the owner a life estate with extra powers and names the people who take afterward. The Department of Revenue addressed its tax treatment in advisement TAA 20B4-004, dated October 16, 2020.

Open the recorded deed and note two things: the powers the owner keeps and the identity of the remainder people. Documents sold under the same label do not always read the same, and what was recorded is what counts. Go through yours slowly before you plan a sale.

Documentary stamp tax on a lady bird deed

In that advisement the answer was no, on the facts presented. The department concluded the deed did not transfer any present beneficial interest, so it owed no documentary stamp tax regardless of consideration.

Those facts carried the result. The life tenants in the request held every power over the land, and a deed giving up some could be analyzed differently. A Florida real estate attorney or the clerk of court can tell you what applies before you record, because the tax is paid at the clerk's office.

A plain life estate deed is on the department's taxable list. What separates the enhanced version is the reasoning that no present beneficial interest moves.

Selling a home held under a lady bird deed

A sale begins with a deed to the buyer signed with the formalities Florida requires, so the first question is who must sign.

Section 689.01 requires a land conveyance to be written and signed before two subscribing witnesses. No seal is needed, and the witnessing can be done by audio-video technology. Whether the named remainder people must also sign depends on the powers written into your deed. The title agent reads the recorded text before agreeing to insure, so raise the question with the agent before you list.

  • Pull the recorded deed from the clerk's official records.
  • Check which powers the deed reserves to the owner, including selling and mortgaging.
  • Find out whether the underwriter will insure with only the owner signing.
  • Expect the sale deed to be taxed at the standard doc stamp rate.

Effect on the property tax bill

Whether the deed counts as a title change drives the tax result. A sale, foreclosure or other transfer of legal or beneficial title resets the assessment to just value on the next January 1 (s. 193.155). Spouse-to-spouse transfers and some transfers at death are exempted.

The advisement reasoned that nothing beneficial passes at signing. Whether the property appraiser's office reads your deed that way is a separate matter, so ask before relying on it. The state's cap chart lists 2.7 percent for 2026, 2.9 percent for 2025 and 3.0 percent for 2024, when CPI ran 3.4 percent and the 3 percent ceiling governed.

The homestead exemption is worth up to $50,000, in two layers. School taxes feel only the first $25,000, while the other $25,000 hits non-school taxes on value over $50,000. Form DR-501 starts it. If you rent the unit or move out, it ends.

Buying a replacement home

An owner who buys again in Florida can port part of the Save Our Homes savings, provided the new homestead is established within three years. The count begins January 1 of the year the old homestead was given up, and the closing date is irrelevant.

Form DR-501T travels with the new DR-501. The new assessed value is reduced by $500,000 or by the old home's just-minus-assessed gap, whichever is smaller (s. 193.155(8)). Changes under chapter 2026-239 start with the 2027 roll, so the appraiser can tell you which rules fit your year.

  • Your buyer's assessment resets to just value after your sale.
  • Homestead filings close March 1.
  • Residence has to exist on January 1.
  • Renting out, moving away or leaving Florida cancels the exemption.

Deed types and doc stamp tax

Deed type drives the tax result, who must sign and what the title insurer will accept.

Deed typeDoc stamp result
Lady bird (enhanced life estate), on the facts in TAA 20B4-004Not subject, regardless of consideration
Life estate deedListed as a taxable deed
Quit claim deedListed as a taxable deed
Agreement or contract for deedListed as a taxable deed

Two rules apply to any taxable deed. Everyone named on the document is liable for the tax, and if one party is exempt a non-exempt party must pay. Deeds are taxable whether or not they are recorded. Recording costs follow section 28.24, which also adds a $1.00 charge for each name beyond four on an instrument.

Documents to line up before listing

The recorded deed answers three questions: who holds the life estate, which powers are reserved, and who receives the property afterward. Bring those answers to the title agent, and to the closing attorney if something is unclear.

  • Government photo identification for each person who will sign the sale deed.
  • The names of two adults who can witness the signing in person or by audio-video link.
  • A payoff statement for any mortgage on the property.
  • Your latest tax bill, to see whether homestead is applied.

Having these ready cuts the time from signed contract to recorded deed. It also keeps the title company from stopping to ask for them.

If the property is held with a co-owner, line up that person's identification and availability for the signing as well. Scheduling two signers across different cities is a common source of delay, and the audio-video option for witnesses does not remove the need for each signer to be present in some form.

Selling fast with a lady bird deed in place

Cash buyers still want clean title. Gather the recorded deed, the legal description and any mortgage payoff before you talk to them.

The closing agent verifies each signer, pays off liens from proceeds and sends the sale deed for recording with its tax. After an owner's death, the deed's own terms and any probate steps decide who signs next, and the underwriter will say which court papers it wants. Recording questions go to the clerk's office.

A cash sale skips a lender's appraisal and underwriting, so the title review of your deed is usually the longest step. Giving the agent the recorded deed on day one is the easiest way to shorten it.

Frequently asked questions

Is a lady bird deed subject to Florida doc stamp tax?

Not on the facts of TAA 20B4-004, dated October 16, 2020, where the life tenants kept every power. The department found no present beneficial interest moved, so nothing was owed. Check your own situation with the clerk or an attorney.

Do I need two witnesses on a lady bird deed?

Yes. Section 689.01 wants the deed in writing with two subscribing witnesses. Using a seal is optional, and the witnesses may join by audio-video.

May a life tenant list and sell the property?

Often, depending on which powers your deed reserves. Let the title company read the recorded deed first, then it can say if your signature is enough or the named remainder people must sign too.

Does a lady bird deed keep my homestead exemption?

Deed type is not what matters. The home must stay your permanent residence, and renting or moving out ends the exemption. A change of title resets the Save Our Homes assessment, so ask the property appraiser how your deed is treated.

Which office records a lady bird deed?

The circuit court clerk in the land's county. Any stamp tax is collected at that counter when the deed is recorded, with the page fees from section 28.24.

Florida Squatters Rights: Adverse Possession and the Sheriff Removal Process

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling a house in Florida?

Do squatters have rights to a Florida house?

Only in a narrow case. A person can eventually claim title by adverse possession, but the statute demands seven years of possession plus paid property taxes, and unlawful occupants face removal long before that. For an owner of a Florida house, the faster tool is the sheriff removal process in section 82.036.

Below are both rules, so you can see why a squatter's claim is weak and how to regain possession. A tenant is different from a squatter, and a lease changes which law applies.

Adverse possession without a deed

Under section 95.18, a claimant needs seven years of actual, continued possession under a claim of title that is not based on a written instrument. The claimant must also meet tax conditions.

  • Pay all outstanding taxes within one year of entering the property.
  • File a return with the county property appraiser within 30 days after that payment.
  • Keep paying taxes for every year of the claim.

Possession counts when the land is protected by a substantial enclosure or cultivated, maintained or improved in a usual manner. The property appraiser mails the return to the record owner and notes the claim on the tax roll, which gives the owner written warning.

Claims based on a written instrument

Adverse possession under color of title also runs seven years, but it starts from a written conveyance, decree or judgment. For possession that began after December 31, 1945, section 95.16 requires the instrument to be recorded with the clerk of the circuit court in the county where the land lies.

The statute lists what counts as possession: usual cultivation or improvement, a substantial enclosure, use for fuel or fencing timber, or partial improvement of a known lot or single farm. Where land is enclosed, only the part included in the written description is treated as possessed.

Is living in a house on an adverse possession claim legal?

Not before the claimant files the return. Occupying a residential structure solely on an adverse possession claim before the return is filed is trespass under section 810.08, and offering the home for lease is theft under section 812.014.

So a person who moves into a vacant house and announces they have rights has not started a legitimate clock. A police report and a sheriff complaint are your next steps. Do not change the locks on someone who holds a lease, or who has received mail there for months, without asking an attorney, because the removal statute fits only a narrow set of facts.

How the sheriff removal process works

The owner or the owner's agent files a verified Complaint to Remove Persons Unlawfully Occupying Residential Real Property with the sheriff. The sheriff then serves a notice to vacate immediately and puts the owner back in possession, if section 82.036's conditions are met.

Those conditions are:

  • The property is residential and not open to the public.
  • No tenancy exists and the occupants are not family of the owner.
  • The owner has told the occupants to leave.
  • No litigation about the property is pending.

A false statement has a price. The occupant can recover damages, including statutory damages of triple the fair market rent, plus costs and attorney fees. Treat the complaint like a sworn court filing.

If the occupant is a tenant or former tenant

Then Florida's landlord and tenant chapter governs, not the squatter statute. For unpaid rent, section 83.56 calls for three days' written notice, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and court-observed holidays, demanding rent or possession.

A tenant who raises a defense other than payment must put the accrued rent into the court registry within five days, again excluding weekends and holidays, or the landlord can obtain a default judgment under section 83.60. After judgment the clerk issues a writ and the sheriff gives 24 hours' posted notice before restoring possession under section 83.62.

What to document before asking the sheriff to act

Keep proof that you own the house and that nobody ever had your permission to stay. A recorded deed and a current property tax bill usually answer the first point, and a written demand to leave answers the second.

  • Dated photos or video of the occupied home.
  • Any message in which you told the occupants to leave.
  • Confirmation that no lease, rent payment or family tie exists.
  • A search of the county court records for any pending case about the house.

Each item lines up with a condition in section 82.036, so the sworn complaint can state facts without guessing. If a court case about the property is open, the sheriff route is unavailable and the attorney handling that case is the person to call.

Effect of a squatter claim on a sale or the tax roll

A return filed with the property appraiser leaves a mark on the tax roll, and buyers and title companies look at the roll and at the official records. If you learn of a filing, tell the closing attorney the same day, because the claim has to be answered before title can be called clean.

Paying the property tax bill on time on a vacant house also takes away part of a claimant's story, since adverse possession rests on the claimant paying the taxes. Owners of empty houses can ask the county property appraiser how to receive notice if a return arrives, and can check the tax collector's records for payments made by someone else.

Vacant houses invite trouble most often in the months after an owner dies or moves. A neighbor, a caretaker or a family member visiting weekly can spot a stranger early. An early report to the sheriff is easier to handle than a long occupancy.

SituationPath
Stranger living in the home, no leaseSheriff complaint
Tenant who has not paid3 day notice, then court
Claimant paying taxes and filing a returnCourt action over title
Claimant with a recorded written instrumentCourt action over title

If you cannot tell which row fits, ask a Florida real estate attorney or the sheriff's civil process unit before serving anything.

Selling a house with an unwanted occupant

Resolve who has the right to be there first, since an occupant with a claim can complicate title and a closing. Owners often pair the sheriff or court step with a sale to a buyer who purchases as is.

Gather the deed, the latest tax bill, any notices you served and any police report. If the occupant files a property appraiser return, tell your attorney and the title company right away, because the claim appears on the tax roll.

Frequently asked questions

How long does adverse possession take in Florida?

Seven years of actual continued possession. The claimant also has to pay taxes and file a return with the property appraiser, so seven years of simply living there does not meet the statute.

Can I call the sheriff on squatters in my Florida home?

Yes, if the facts fit section 82.036: residential property, no tenancy, not family, you told them to leave, and no pending litigation. You submit a verified complaint and the sheriff serves the notice.

What if I lie on the sheriff complaint?

The occupant can seek damages, including statutory damages of triple the fair market rent, costs and attorney fees. File only with accurate facts.

Is a tenant who stopped paying a squatter?

No. A tenant falls under the landlord and tenant chapter, which starts with written notice and a court case. The sheriff acts after a judgment and a writ.

Does the claimant have to record anything?

Under color of title, the written instrument must be recorded with the circuit court clerk. Without color of title, the claimant files a return with the county property appraiser.

A Florida landlord can end a tenancy for unpaid rent with a written 3-day notice that excludes weekends and legal holidays, and must go to county court to recover possession. Landlords cannot lock tenants out. This guide summarizes Chapter 83 as the Florida Statutes show it.

Selling a house in Florida?

The steps in a Florida eviction

A Florida eviction runs in five stages: written notice, a court complaint, the tenant's response, a judgment, and removal by the sheriff. Each stage has its own clock under Chapter 83 of the Florida Statutes.

The order matters. A landlord who changes the locks, shuts off the water or carries out the tenant's belongings has skipped the court stage, and that shortcut can bring its own claims. The slow, documented path is the one that ends with a writ in hand.

Owners who plan to sell have to think about timing too. Every stage adds days, and a buyer will want a closing date the court calendar can support.

Before going to court

The landlord starts by serving a written notice that fits the problem. For unpaid rent that's a three day notice, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and court observed legal holidays, under section 83.56(3).

  • Lease breaches the tenant can fix: seven days to cure after delivery.
  • Breaches that can't be fixed: seven days to vacate.
  • Same breach again within 12 months: suit may go ahead without a new notice.

The notice may be mailed, handed over, emailed under section 83.505 where that applies, or left at the home when the tenant is away. The lease can't waive any of this. Our page on Florida eviction notices goes through each notice type in more detail.

What the tenant must do after service

A tenant who wants to fight on any ground other than payment has to move fast. Within five days of service, again excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, the tenant must deposit the accrued rent into the court registry or ask the court to set the rent. Section 83.60(2) covers this.

Missing the deadline waives every defense except payment, and the landlord can ask for an immediate default judgment. Many cases end right here, since a tenant who can't post the money loses the chance to argue.

The deposit isn't a penalty. It keeps the rent available to the landlord while the court decides. A tenant who has paid in full has a defense that needs no deposit, and should bring proof of payment to the hearing.

Partial rent taken during the case

Accepting some rent after serving the three day notice doesn't end the case, but it comes with rules. Under section 83.56, the landlord must hand the tenant a receipt stating the balance still due, pay the partial rent into the court registry when filing the complaint, or serve a new three day notice.

A landlord who ignores this and simply cashes the check gives the tenant an argument that the notice was waived. If you're unsure which path to take, ask the clerk of the county court where you plan to file, or consult a Florida attorney before accepting any money.

Tenants should keep proof of every payment. A receipt, bank record or money order stub can settle a dispute over what was paid and when.

From judgment to removal

Once the court rules for the landlord, the clerk issues a writ of possession to the sheriff. The sheriff posts a notice at the home, and after 24 hours puts the landlord in possession. Weekends and holidays don't stay that 24 hour period under section 83.62.

Only the sheriff executes the writ. A landlord tempted to speed things along by showing up with a moving crew is outside the statute. Keep the writ, the posting date and the date of possession in the file, since a title company may ask for them.

Periodic tenancies

Not every removal needs a default. When a tenancy has no set end date, the landlord can end it with advance notice instead of proving a breach. Section 83.57 sets the length by rental period: at least 30 days for month to month and quarter to quarter, 60 days for year to year, and 7 days for week to week.

The notice has to come before the period ends. If the tenant stays past the end date, the landlord files in court and the usual stages apply, from the tenant's response through judgment and the sheriff's writ.

For an owner who wants to sell a house with no one inside, this is often the cleanest route, since it doesn't depend on a payment or lease problem. The price is waiting out the notice period.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Papers to keep

  • The lease and any renewals or amendments.
  • The notice as served and the proof of how it was delivered.
  • A ledger of rent charged and received.
  • The court complaint, the tenant's answer, and any registry deposit record.
  • The judgment, writ of possession and sheriff's posting date.

A buyer's lender or title agent may ask for these when a rental sale follows an eviction. One folder for all of it saves time at closing.

Eviction clocks at a glance

Florida eviction clocks from Chapter 83
StepPeriodSection
Rent demand notice3 days, excluding weekends and court observed holidays83.56(3)
Curable breach notice7 days to cure83.56
Incurable breach notice7 days to vacate83.56
Tenant deposit or motion to set rent5 days after service, excluding weekends and holidays83.60(2)
Sheriff posting before possession24 hours83.62
Month to month end notice30 days before period ends83.57

Counting rules differ from step to step, so read the text of each section before you rely on a date.

Selling a rental house during an eviction

An owner may market a property with an eviction in progress, but a buyer who closes with an occupant still inside inherits the problem. Most buyers who finance will want vacant possession, so an unfinished case tends to push the closing out.

The practical options:

  • Finish the eviction, then list the home with the keys in hand.
  • Offer the home to an investor who buys with the tenant in place.
  • Where the tenancy has no end date and the tenant isn't in default, use the notice periods in section 83.57 and time the sale to the end of the period.

A Florida attorney or the clerk of the county court can confirm local filing steps and fees. Forms vary a little by county, so ask the clerk where you file.

Where evictions go wrong

Most failed evictions trace back to early defects. The notice gave the wrong number of days, it wasn't delivered a way the statute allows, or the landlord took partial rent after serving it without following the receipt, registry or new notice rule in section 83.56.

Self help is the second trouble spot. Changing locks or removing a tenant's property outside the writ turns a landlord who was in the right into a defendant. Keep every date, copy and receipt, and let the sheriff carry out the final step.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a Florida eviction take?

The statutes set short clocks: 3 or 7 days for notices, 5 days for the tenant's deposit and 24 hours for the sheriff's posting. Court scheduling decides the rest, so ask the clerk of the county court for local timing.

Does the tenant have to pay money into the court?

Yes, if the tenant raises any defense other than payment. The accrued rent goes into the court registry, or a motion to determine rent is filed, within 5 days after service, excluding weekends and legal holidays.

Who carries out the eviction in Florida?

The sheriff. After judgment the clerk issues a writ, and the sheriff posts a 24 hour notice before putting the landlord back in possession.

Can I accept part of the rent after serving the notice?

Only with care. The landlord must give a receipt showing the balance, pay the partial amount into the court registry when filing, or serve a new three day notice.

Can I sell the house with a tenant still living in it?

Yes, but the buyer takes the situation as it stands. Closing is usually faster once the tenancy has ended or a buyer agrees to take the home occupied.

Florida Summary Administration: Small Estate Rules and Selling an Inherited Home

Cash Home Buyers in Florida
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Summary Administration sale
  • Turn the Florida Summary Administration offer down and you owe us nothing

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Florida summary administration is available when the estate subject to administration is within the statutory limit or the decedent has been dead more than 2 years. The statute currently shows a $150,000 limit after a 2026 amendment, not the older $75,000 figure.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

What summary administration is

Summary administration is the shortened court process Florida offers for a small or old estate, and it can clear title to an inherited house without a full probate. The rules sit in chapter 735 of the Florida Statutes, in the part titled Probate Code: Small Estates.

The court enters one order assigning the estate to the people entitled to it. A title company reads that order when a beneficiary wants to sell the house. If you inherited a Florida home and the paperwork feels heavy, talk to a probate attorney before anything is listed.

Does your estate qualify?

An estate qualifies if its value is $150,000 or less after exempt property is set aside, or if the person has been dead for more than two years. The statute was amended in 2026, so check the current limit with the clerk or an attorney before relying on an older figure such as $75,000.

  • The decedent may be a Florida resident or a nonresident with Florida assets.
  • Exempt property under the Florida Constitution and statutes is left out of the value count.
  • A will can block the route if it directs administration as chapter 733 requires.

A house is often the largest asset, so the size test depends on whether the home counts as exempt homestead. That turns on the facts, which is why the court and the clerk matter more than any online estimate.

Who files the petition and who signs

Any beneficiary, or the person a will nominates as personal representative, can file the petition. The surviving spouse and the beneficiaries must sign and verify it.

A beneficiary who receives a full share under the proposed distribution does not have to join, but still receives formal notice. When a signer has died, is a minor, or lacks capacity, a representative or guardian signs instead, and a person who bought a beneficiary's interest may sign in that beneficiary's place. For a family spread across several states, gathering signatures is usually the slowest part.

What the court order does for a buyer

The order allows immediate distribution and protects a purchaser. Someone who pays value to a person assigned the property takes it free of the decedent's creditors and of the claims of a spouse and other beneficiaries.

That protection is why a title insurer will usually accept the order as the link in the chain of title. There are limits you should know about:

  • Before the order, the petitioner must search for known or reasonably findable creditors, serve them with the petition and provide for payment as far as assets allow.
  • Heirs who receive property are personally liable for a pro rata share of lawful claims, up to the value they actually received.
  • After two years from the death, the estate and its recipients are no longer liable for claims unless proceedings to enforce them began.
  • An heir left out of the order can pursue the people who obtained it and may recover attorney fees.

Estates that need no administration

An estate needs none when it holds only exempt personal property plus a small amount of other personal property. The ceiling for the non-exempt part is preferred funeral expenses and reasonable medical and hospital costs from the last 60 days of the final illness.

The court may then authorize a transfer on an informal application. A house rarely fits this track, because real estate is neither exempt personal property nor small in value. This route is for bank accounts and vehicles. Use summary or formal administration for land.

Creditor deadlines and selling an inherited home

Creditors lose their claims once the filing deadline passes, which makes the deadline a practical date for heirs. A claim is barred unless filed by the later of three months after first publication of the notice to creditors or 30 days after service on a creditor who had to be served.

Summary administration runs on its own two year outer limit, described above. Ask the probate attorney which clock applies to your file, since publication dates and service dates vary by case.

Estate tax and deed tax on an inherited house

Florida levies no estate tax for deaths after December 31, 2004. Since July 1, 2023, personal representatives skip Forms DR-312 and DR-313. Federal rules are separate.

Documentary stamp tax is the cost that surprises heirs. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is not taxable, yet estate planning transfers of Florida real property have no specific exemption. When the heirs later deed the house to a buyer, that deed is taxable in the ordinary way, and the rate per $100 differs in Miami-Dade, so confirm the rate for your county.

Homestead and the will

Florida homestead cannot be left by will when the owner is survived by a spouse or a minor child, with one exception: it may go to a spouse when no minor child exists. A trust disposition is treated the same way as a devise.

So a will that names a sibling as heir to the family home may not control who inherits it. Before anyone signs a sale contract, a probate attorney should confirm who actually holds title, because a buyer needs the right signatures on the deed.

First steps and records before a sale

Collect the death certificate, the will if there is one, the deed to the house and the latest tax bill. Then compare the estate with the thresholds above and decide between summary and formal administration.

Small estate routes in Florida
RouteWhen it fits
Summary administrationNon-exempt estate of $150,000 or less, or dead more than 2 years
No administrationOnly exempt property and limited personal property
Formal administrationEstates outside both routes

Once the court has ruled, the heirs sign a deed and the county recording office files it in the Official Records. The clerk charges by the page, with trust fund and technology add-ons, so ask for the total before you go.

What a cash sale skips

Heirs who do not want to repair or clean out an inherited house can sell it as-is for cash after the court order is in hand. That route skips listing prep, showings and a buyer's lender appraisal, though the title company still needs the order, the deed and the signatures of everyone who holds an interest. Ask the probate attorney for a certified copy of the order, and keep the death certificate, the will and the tax bill in one folder so the closing is not delayed by a missing page.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Florida summary administration limit?

The limit is $150,000 in non-exempt value, or the decedent having been dead more than two years. The statute was amended in 2026, so confirm the current figure with the clerk of the court.

Can I sell an inherited Florida house before the court order?

Usually not, because the heirs need an order or other proof of who holds title. A buyer's title company decides what it will accept, so ask it early and ask the probate attorney who must sign.

Do all heirs have to sign the petition?

Most do. The surviving spouse and the beneficiaries sign, except a beneficiary receiving a full distributive share, who is not required to join but must receive formal notice.

Can creditors still collect after summary administration?

Yes, for a limited time. Heirs share liability for lawful claims up to what they received, and the exposure ends two years after death unless enforcement proceedings began.

Does Florida have an estate tax on a house passing to heirs?

No. Florida has no estate tax for deaths after 2004. Doc stamp tax can still apply to deeds, so ask the clerk or an attorney how your deed is treated.

Florida Inheritance Tax and Estate Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Florida
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Inheritance Tax and Estate Tax sale
  • Turn the Florida Inheritance Tax and Estate Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Inherited a Florida House? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Does Florida have an inheritance or estate tax?

Florida taxes neither. The state estate tax ended with a federal change for anyone dying after December 31, 2004, and as of July 1, 2023 representatives skip Forms DR-312 and DR-313. Simply inheriting a house here creates no state bill.

Three other costs can still arise. One is federal estate tax on very large estates. Another is federal tax on gain when the house sells. The last is stamp tax on a deed that moves title for value.

Federal estate tax threshold

Only the largest estates owe federal tax. An estate return is due once the gross estate, together with lifetime taxable gifts and the gift tax exemption used, goes over the line for the death year.

Year of deathEstate return filing threshold
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

Debts, administration costs and anything left to a surviving spouse or a qualified charity are deductible. A surviving spouse who files on time can carry over exemption the first estate did not use.

Your basis in an inherited house

Your starting figure for gain is normally what the house was worth when the owner died, which replaces the owner's purchase price. Publication 551 lets the personal representative pick a later valuation date instead.

If the estate files Form 706, the executor usually hands each beneficiary a Schedule A (Form 8971) listing the reported value, which some must adopt as basis. With no such form, the appraisal used for state inheritance or transmission tax can stand in.

There is one exception. Appreciated property that you or your spouse gave the decedent in the year before death keeps the decedent's adjusted basis.

Keep any appraisal made around the death in the estate file, and have a CPA relate it to your sale price.

Who reports the sale income

The heir reports it on a federal return. A sale close to the stepped-up value tends to leave little gain, while a sale well above it can leave more. A CPA can tell you whether any other return applies.

How a deed is taxed when an inherited house changes hands

How title moves decides the tax. When a personal representative signs the deed under a probated will, no stamp tax is due. Warranty, special warranty, quit claim and life estate deeds are all taxable.

Outside Miami-Dade a taxable deed owes 70 cents per $100 of consideration, and a mortgage or other encumbrance counts as consideration whether or not the buyer assumes it. No exemption exists merely because a transfer is estate planning. Giving away a mortgaged house can therefore be taxed with no cash exchanged (s. 201.02).

  • Probated will: the deed signed by the representative is the untaxed route.
  • Quitclaim between heirs: taxable if debt attaches.
  • All parties to a taxable deed are liable, whatever the contract says about who pays.

Probate rules that set the pace

Timing comes from three statutes. Summary administration suits an estate whose non-exempt assets are $150,000 or less, or one where the owner died over two years ago (s. 735.201). Creditors file by the later of three months from first publication of notice and 30 days from service, when service was required (s. 733.702). If only exempt or minor personal property is left, a court may permit transfer with no administration at all (s. 735.301).

Homestead complicates things. If a spouse or minor child survives, the home cannot be left by will, so the will may not decide who holds title. The spouse then has six months to choose a half interest in place of a life estate (s. 732.401). Ask the title insurer what it needs before you list.

Tax accrues the whole time the estate is open. A transfer at death can also reset just value on the next January 1, absent an exception.

Property taxes after the owner dies

Nothing pauses the tax. January 1 fixes the assessment, and bills come from the tax collector in November, with discounts of 4 percent, 3, 2 and 1 from November through February. An open estate is no excuse for skipping them.

The homestead exemption rests on permanent residence, so it stops when the house is no longer the owner's permanent home. Following a death, the estate or heir should ask the appraiser how the parcel will be listed next year.

Passing title sets the parcel back to just value on the next January 1, with exceptions for spousal transfers and certain transfers at death. Expect a buyer from the estate to see the reset.

Spreading out a tax bill

Heirs have a few options, though not all will fit. Paying in installments means applying to the tax collector by May 1 of the assessment year (s. 197.222). Part payments ahead of the delinquency date are up to the collector (s. 197.374). A homestead deferral on Form DR-570 is filed by March 31 following the assessment year and turns on household income.

Who lives in the house decides which option applies, because homestead needs permanent residence. An heir who lives elsewhere should ask the tax collector what suits a non-homestead parcel, and pay before April 1 so the bill never goes delinquent.

Have the collector confirm any deal in writing and file it with the estate records. The closing agent can then show the buyer nothing is owed.

Paperwork to have ready

  • A date-of-death appraisal or a Schedule A, if issued, to document basis.
  • Letters or a summary administration order showing who may sign.
  • A recorded spousal election, if one was made on homestead.
  • The newest tax bill and any deferral papers.
  • The reasoning for how each deed is taxed or exempt under chapter 201.

Florida has no estate tax return to chase down. Form 706 comes into play only for estates over the IRS line for the death year.

Heirs who cannot agree on a price or buyer may end up in front of a judge. Raise the disagreement early, since a vacant house keeps generating tax, insurance and upkeep bills.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Order of work for an heir

Authority comes first: court letters, or a summary administration order, plus any recorded spousal election when homestead is involved. With that settled, hunt down the appraisal made near the death or the Schedule A, so your tax adviser can set your basis. After that, request the latest tax bill and look for open deferrals or installment plans.

Then choose the deed form. When the personal representative signs under a probated will, no stamp tax is owed. A quit claim among heirs may be taxed. Have the closing agent confirm the treatment a few days ahead.

Co-heirs would do well to put in writing who signs, who gets the check and how repairs are split. One holdout can freeze a closing. When the buyer pays cash, no lender appraisal or underwriting intervenes, so these papers end up setting the date.

Selling quickly or holding the house

Carrying costs usually settle this question. The tax bill arrives every November, delinquency starts April 1, and a vacant house still needs insurance, utilities and repairs. Against that, a sale near the day-of-death value usually leaves little gain to report. A cash buyer can close without a lender's timeline, which helps when carrying costs are the worry.

Slow probate leaves the tax picture as it was. It does not remove the November bill, and it does not postpone the reset in assessed value that follows a transfer of title. Compare the monthly carrying cost with the likely sale price, and ask a CPA or attorney how your facts fit before you commit to a buyer.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Florida inheritance tax?

No. The state's estate tax ended for anyone dying after December 31, 2004, and no inheritance levy took its place. Getting a house from an estate creates no state tax by itself.

When would federal estate tax apply to a house I inherit?

Only when the whole estate is above the IRS threshold, $15,000,000 for a 2026 death. The estate pays it, not the heir, and most estates stay under.

What basis do I use on an inherited Florida house?

Usually the home's worth at the owner's death, or a later valuation date if the estate elected one. If an estate return was filed, Schedule A (Form 8971) reports the number.

Is a personal representative's deed taxed?

No stamp tax applies when the deed follows a probated will. Quit claim and warranty deeds are taxable, at the 70 cent rate used outside Miami-Dade.

Who reports gain on an inherited house sale?

The heir reports it on a federal return. A stepped-up basis typically keeps gain small on a prompt sale, and a CPA can confirm that.

A Florida deed must be signed in the presence of two subscribing witnesses (Sec. 689.01), and the clerk will record it only if it carries printed names and post-office addresses. Documentary stamp tax on deeds is 70 cents per $100 of consideration.

Selling a house in Florida?

What a Florida warranty deed does

A warranty deed moves title to land and carries the grantor's promise that the title is good. The statutory form has the grantor "fully warrant the title to said land, and will defend the same against the lawful claims of all persons whomsoever."

That promise is what sets it apart from a quit claim deed, which hands over whatever interest the grantor holds without vouching for it. Buyers who pay full price, and the lenders behind them, usually expect the stronger form. Section 689.02 supplies sample wording, and a deed may be built on it.

What makes the deed valid and recordable

Under s. 689.01 the deed must be a signed writing with two subscribing witnesses present. A seal is optional, and witnesses may appear by audio-video link.

Getting it onto the public record takes more. Section 695.26 bars the clerk from filing the paper unless it shows:

  • Each signer's name printed beneath the signature, with a post-office address.
  • The person who drafted it, named with a mailing address.
  • Each witness's name printed beneath the signature, with an address.
  • The name of the notary or other officer taking the acknowledgment, printed under that signature.
  • Empty space in the upper right corner, larger on page one, for clerk stamps.
  • Every buyer's name and address, written out.

Out-of-state signings, court orders and wills are carved out of that section. And if a clerk accepts a deed that misses one of these steps, the recording and its constructive notice still stand.

Parcel number on the deed

The statutory form has a blank for the property appraiser's parcel identification number. A missing or wrong number does not void the deed.

Section 689.02(2) asks that the number be entered before recording when it is available. It is not part of the legal description and cannot replace it. Copy the legal description exactly from your prior deed or a survey, then add the parcel number as a convenience for the clerk and the appraiser.

What stamp tax applies to a Florida deed?

The deed rate is 70 cents for each $100 of consideration. Miami-Dade runs on a different schedule: 60 cents, plus a 45 cent surtax that does not apply to a document moving only a single-family home.

Consideration is read widely. It covers cash, a released debt, and any loan secured on the land, assumed or not, so a deed reciting a token sum can still draw tax on the mortgage balance.

Everyone on the deed answers for the tax whatever the contract says, and an exempt party's share shifts to a non-exempt one. An unrecorded deed is not outside the tax.

Which transfers escape deed tax

Few do. The Department of Revenue names no exemption aimed at estate planning.

Deed types and documentary stamp tax
DocumentTaxable?
Warranty, special warranty, quit claim, trustee and life estate deedsTaxable
Deed in lieu of foreclosure, contract for deed, certificate of titleTaxable
Deed from a personal representative acting under a probated willNot taxable
Spouse-to-spouse homestead deed backed only by a mortgage; marital home deed in a divorceExempt under s. 201.02(7)

Lady bird deeds get separate handling. In an October 2020 advisement, the department treated one, where the life tenants kept full powers, as passing no present beneficial interest and so outside stamp tax. Whether your deed fits that pattern is a question for a Florida attorney.

Clerk recording charges

Section 28.24(13) fixes these fees, and they come on top of stamp tax.

  • Page one costs $5.00 and each later page $4.00 (standard size, up to 14 by 8.5 inches).
  • An extra $1.00 per name after the fourth.
  • A records modernization trust fund fee: $1.00 for page one, $0.50 afterward.
  • An additional $4 per page technology charge.

Call the clerk's office for the total on your page count.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Other stamp taxes around a sale

Mortgage paperwork is taxed apart from the deed. The rate is 35 cents per $100 of the amount secured, with the tax on a note capped at $2,450 and no cap on mortgages.

After a foreclosure sale, the certificate of title is taxed on the best bid made (s. 201.02(9)). In an ordinary sale between private parties, the deed tax is usually the main figure. Ask your closing agent whether the buyer's new loan adds charges of its own.

Preparing the deed before closing

Pull the pieces together early. A clerk can reject an instrument at the counter, and the closing then slips.

  • Take the legal description from your vesting deed and copy it character for character.
  • Confirm how each grantor's name appears in the record and use the same spelling.
  • Line up two adult witnesses and a notary for signing day, or ask the title company about remote witnessing.
  • Print every name and mailing address where the statute calls for one.
  • Leave the top right corner of each page clear for the clerk.

Then confirm with the closing agent what stamp tax will be due and who funds it. If the sale is a cash deal with no lender, there is no loan paperwork to coordinate, but the deed rules are the same.

Which deed fits a sale and which a family transfer?

For an arm's-length sale at market price, buyers and lenders generally look for a warranty deed because it carries the title promise. A quit claim deed passes only what the grantor owns. It is common between relatives or to fix a name on the record, though it is still on the department's taxable list.

A contract for deed is taxable too, and the buyer under a recorded contract for deed is one of the people notified before a tax deed sale. Section 689.01 reaches any conveyance of a freehold or of a term longer than one year, so a long lease needs the same two witnesses.

Property taxes after the deed is recorded

Title passing by sale, foreclosure or any other route counts as a change of ownership for assessment. Just value applies from the next January 1, and the seller's Save Our Homes cap stays behind.

Spousal transfers and some transfers at death are carved out. A quitclaim to a relative is not an exception just because no money changes hands. Buyers should file for their own homestead exemption with the county property appraiser by March 1, and should look into portability if they held a homestead elsewhere in the state.

Frequently asked questions

Do both spouses have to sign a Florida warranty deed?

Not always, but a married owner should confirm whether the home is homestead before signing. Spousal joinder rules for homestead are a question for a Florida title attorney or title company. Every signer must still meet the two-witness and printed-name rules.

Can I use a warranty deed to give a house to my child?

Yes, but the transfer is a change of ownership for assessment and can carry stamp tax on any mortgage balance. No estate planning exemption exists, so talk with an attorney before choosing a deed type.

Who covers the stamp tax on a deed?

The contract can assign it, though the state looks to every party on the deed. The clerk collects it at recording.

Is a deed valid if the clerk's recording was imperfect?

Generally yes. Section 695.26(4) says a clerk's failure to follow the recording checklist does not impair the recording or its constructive notice. Fix defects anyway, because title companies will flag them.

Can a deed in lieu replace a warranty deed?

No. A deed in lieu is how a borrower hands a property back to a lender, and it is taxable. A warranty deed is the normal choice in an arm's-length sale.

A Florida quitclaim deed must meet the same writing and two-witness rule as other deeds, and documentary stamp tax applies at 70 cents per $100 of consideration. A deed between spouses or former spouses in a divorce for the marital home is excepted.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

How a quitclaim works

Signing a quitclaim in Florida passes along the signer's share, whatever it turns out to be, with zero assurance that the share is clean. A lien, an unknown heir or a boundary dispute stays attached, and the person receiving the deed absorbs it.

Because nothing is promised, these deeds turn up mostly inside families: a husband adding his wife to title, a parent funding a family trust, one spouse leaving title after a divorce. A stranger paying market price normally expects a warranty deed or special warranty deed, and the buyer's lender or title insurer will often demand one.

Calling the instrument a quitclaim does not loosen Florida's signing, recording or tax rules. They apply just as they would to any other deed.

Signing and recording requirements

Florida wants the deed written out and signed with two subscribing witnesses watching. A seal is not required, and the witnesses can attend by audio-video link.

Recording is pickier. The circuit court clerk takes the instrument only when it carries all of these:

  • a printed name and post-office address for every signer;
  • the name and address of whoever prepared it, who has to be a natural person;
  • printed names and addresses for the witnesses, with any notary's printed name under the notary signature;
  • an empty box in the top right corner reserved for the clerk, 3 by 3 inches on the first page and 1 by 3 inches after that;
  • the name and address of the grantee.

Instruments signed outside Florida, wills, plats and court orders are exempt from this list. If a clerk records a deed with a gap, the recording holds up, yet the counter is where such a deed gets refused. Run down the list before you drive over.

Documentary stamp tax

Yes. Quit claim deeds are taxed just like warranty, special warranty, trustee's and life estate deeds, at 70 cents for every $100 of consideration.

Consideration reaches beyond cash. Money paid, debt forgiven, and any mortgage or encumbrance on the parcel all count, even when the grantee never assumes the loan. Giving a house away with a loan still on it can therefore leave a taxable base.

All parties to the instrument share liability regardless of who promised to pay, and when one party is exempt, the bill lands on a party who is not. You settle up at the clerk's window as the deed is recorded. A taxable deed that never gets recorded still owes the tax directly to the state.

There is no separate exemption for estate planning. Putting your own home into a revocable trust by deed may still be taxed, so ask a Florida attorney or the clerk before you sign. Families often assume a gift deed costs nothing at the counter, and that assumption is where an unexpected bill comes from.

Exempt transfers and recording fees

The tax has narrow escape hatches. A homestead deed between spouses escapes it when the only consideration is a mortgage, and so does a deed giving up the marital home in a divorce. Deeds signed by a personal representative under a probated will are not taxed either.

Recording is billed separately. Here is the schedule.

Nobody can quote the total without seeing the deed. Pages and names drive it, so phone your county clerk for a figure on your own deed.

Effect on your property tax bill

Your tax bill may change. In Florida, a sale, a foreclosure or any other transfer of legal or beneficial title is a change of ownership. Assessed value then goes back to just value the next January 1, absent an exception.

The exceptions cover a transfer where the same person stays entitled to the benefit, a transfer between spouses, and a corrective deed. Someone who has held the house longest, with the lowest assessed value, risks the biggest jump from an accidental reset. Sorting this out before the deed is signed is far cheaper than explaining a surprise assessment afterward.

The homestead exemption is a different matter. You file Form DR-501 with the property appraiser by March 1, and the house has to be your permanent home on January 1. Before adding another name to a homestead deed, speak with the appraiser.

When to use a different deed

A buyer who pays real money wants protection, and a quitclaim gives none. Title insurers tend to hesitate before insuring a purchase that rests on one.

Owners tend to get stuck in these situations:

  • Several heirs hold the house and one of them signs alone. A quitclaim passes only that heir's share.
  • A mortgage remains on the property. The deed leaves the loan in place, and the lender is not held to the transfer.
  • A relative goes on the deed to dodge probate. Because the transfer takes effect at once, that relative becomes a co-owner and must sign any sale.
  • The owner wants to keep control during life. The enhanced life estate deed is built for that.

On that last point, advisement TAA 20B4-004 from October 2020 looked at one lady bird deed and found that no present beneficial interest passed, so no documentary stamp tax applied. The result depended on those exact facts. Confirm how it fits yours.

Selling when title is messy

Before choosing any instrument, find out who legally owns the house. Then match each gap in title to the deed that closes it. A quitclaim can take a cooperative person off title. It cannot conjure ownership that nobody had.

When several heirs inherit, the probate court generally has to approve the transfer. Delinquent taxes or a lien get paid out of the sale. A buyer who accepts the house as it stands can absorb repairs and clutter, though a missing signature will still halt a closing.

Bring the deeds, any mortgage statement, the latest tax bill and a list of everyone who might have an interest. With those in hand, a title company can tell you fast what else it requires. Once every signature is lined up, a cash sale as-is skips the listing, the showings and a buyer's lender appraisal.

Before you go to the clerk

A short routine saves a rejected filing and a second trip. Check that the new owner's full name and address appear on the deed, that both witnesses printed their names and addresses, and that the first page has its reserved corner empty. Decide in advance who is paying the documentary stamp tax and bring the amount, because the clerk collects it when the deed is recorded.

If the property has a mortgage, call the lender before you transfer anything and ask whether the loan allows it. If a family member is joining title on a homestead, call the property appraiser first about the January 1 reset and the March 1 exemption filing. Keep a copy of the signed deed and the recording receipt in the same folder as your closing papers, since a buyer's title company will ask to see where the chain of ownership stands.

Frequently asked questions

Does Florida require an attorney to prepare a quitclaim deed?

No law makes an attorney a condition of signing, but the deed must satisfy the two-witness rule and the recording checklist. Tax and title consequences follow, so many owners hire a Florida attorney or title company anyway.

Who is liable for doc stamps on a quitclaim deed?

Every party to the instrument is liable, whichever party agreed to pay. The clerk collects the tax at recording.

What rate applies to a Florida deed?

The statute sets 70 cents per $100 of consideration. Miami-Dade County has a different base rate plus a surtax, and the surtax is not due on a document transferring only a single-family dwelling.

Can a quitclaim deed change my homestead assessment?

Yes. A transfer of title counts as a change of ownership unless a statutory exception applies, and the property resets to just value the following January 1.

Is a quitclaim deed the same as a lady bird deed?

No. A quitclaim deed passes the signer's interest now, while a lady bird deed keeps lifetime control with the owner. The 2020 advisement on lady bird deeds turned on the powers the life tenants kept.

When a Florida owner dies without a valid will, the surviving spouse takes the entire intestate estate if the decedent left no descendants, and shares change when descendants exist. Undevised homestead follows its own rule.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

Who gets the house when there is no will

Chapter 732 of the Florida Statutes sets the order. Spouse and descendants come first, then parents, then siblings, then more distant kin. Who actually takes depends on who survives, and a house that counts as homestead follows extra rules.

"Intestate" means the owner died without a valid will, or with a will that leaves the property out. In that case the Probate Code names the people who take title. A sale still needs someone with court-given authority to sign the deed, so the order of heirs mostly tells you who receives the proceeds and who must agree.

The surviving spouse's share

The answer turns on the children. Section 732.102 gives the spouse the whole intestate estate in some families and half in others.

  • No surviving descendants of the decedent: the spouse takes everything.
  • Every descendant of the decedent is also the spouse's descendant, and the spouse has no others: the spouse takes everything.
  • At least one descendant of the decedent is not the spouse's: the spouse takes one-half.
  • All the decedent's descendants are shared with the spouse, but the spouse also has descendants from outside the marriage: the spouse takes one-half.

Blended families are where disputes begin. If the spouse has children from an earlier relationship, the share drops to half even when every child of the decedent is also the spouse's child.

Who inherits next, or when there is no spouse

Section 732.103 sets a ladder. A step applies only when every step above it is empty. The whole estate, or whatever the spouse does not take, moves down this list.

  1. The decedent's descendants.
  2. The father and mother equally, or the survivor of them.
  3. Brothers and sisters, with the descendants of any who died.
  4. Grandparents, then aunts, uncles and their descendants, split between the paternal and maternal sides, half to each.
  5. Kindred of the last deceased spouse, as if that spouse had survived and then died without a will.

If one side of the family has no living kin, the estate goes to the other side.

The family home with a spouse and children

Without an election, the spouse holds a life estate and the children hold the remainder. This comes from section 732.401, which applies to homestead the owner did not leave by a valid devise.

The remainder is vested in the descendants alive at death, divided per stirpes. A life tenant can live in the house but cannot deliver full title to a buyer alone, so these homes often stall at sale time.

A spouse may pick a different split instead: half of the property as a tenant in common, with the descendants taking the other half. Timing is strict. The election has to happen inside 6 months of the death, while the spouse is still living. Once made it is final. The spouse records a sworn notice of election with the clerk of the home's county. For an incapacitated spouse, the attorney in fact or guardian first needs court approval, and that petition is also bound by the 6 months.

Property held as tenants by the entireties, or with a co-owner under a survivorship arrangement, falls outside this section.

How heirs sell an inherited house

The usual path is to open a probate estate, get a personal representative appointed by the court, and let that person sign the deed. A shorter court procedure exists for small estates.

Section 735.201 allows summary administration when non-exempt assets total no more than $150,000, or when two years have gone by since the death. If just exempt property and a limited amount of other personal property are left, section 735.301 can let a court approve a transfer with no full administration. A house rarely fits either, so ask a probate attorney or the clerk's probate desk.

Creditors can only file for so long. Section 733.702 bars any claim that misses the later of two deadlines: 3 months from the first publication of the notice to creditors, or 30 days from when a creditor owed direct service gets it. Before closing, buyers and title companies check where that clock stands, and look for recorded letters of administration or an order.

Tax and deed costs when heirs sell

A sale brings three cost items: deed tax, recording charges and a change in property tax. There is no state estate tax to plan around, since it ended for deaths after 2004, and the DR-312 and DR-313 filings stopped in July 2023.

The estate's deed to a buyer is taxable. Section 201.02 puts the tax at 70 cents on each $100 of consideration, with all parties liable no matter who the contract says pays. Estate planning earns no special exemption, which means a quitclaim between siblings may be taxed. The one clear exception is the personal representative's deed under a probated will, which is not taxed.

Section 28.24 sets the clerk's recording charges. Call the clerk with your deed's page count to get the total.

For property tax, a change in title resets the assessment to just value the next January 1, except for certain transfers at death. An heir who rents the home out loses homestead. Call the appraiser to see how the parcel will be treated.

Documents the title company will ask for

Plan on handing over the death certificate, court letters or a summary administration order, and the will if one exists. A spouse who made the six-month election should supply the recorded notice. With no election on record, bring proof of that, so the insurer knows what interest the spouse keeps.

Each heir who takes an interest has to be identified. A simple family tree may need little more than an affidavit, while a blended family usually means more paper. Begin early, because chasing a missing signature is what slows most inherited sales.

Even in an all-cash deal, with no lender in the picture, the title company wants every one of these papers before it insures the deed.

Frequently asked questions

Does a surviving spouse always inherit the whole house in Florida?

No. A spouse gets everything only if the decedent had no descendants or every descendant is also the spouse's. When one descendant is not, section 732.102 limits the spouse to one-half. On homestead with a spouse and descendants, section 732.401 normally gives the spouse a life estate, not full title.

Can a surviving spouse choose half of the homestead instead of a life estate?

Yes. The spouse can elect an undivided half share, held in common with the descendants. The election must come within 6 months of death while the spouse is alive, is final, and is recorded as a sworn notice with the clerk of the home's county.

Who inherits if there is no spouse and no children?

Parents take in equal shares, or one parent takes alone if the other has died. Failing parents, siblings and their descendants inherit, followed by the grandparent and aunt and uncle lines, split half to the paternal and half to the maternal side.

Is summary administration available for a house?

It can be. Section 735.201 allows it for non-exempt estates of $150,000 or less, or when the owner died over 2 years ago. Your house may or may not fit, so ask the probate clerk or an attorney.

Is there a Florida estate tax on inherited homes?

No state estate tax applies to deaths after 2004, and Forms DR-312 and DR-313 are no longer filed. Stamp tax can still reach a deed, though a probated-will deed from a personal representative is not taxed.

How probate works for a Florida home

Probate is the court-supervised step that gives someone legal authority over a dead owner's property. A Florida house usually cannot be sold or retitled by an heir until that authority exists. The court names a personal representative, who handles notices, creditor claims and the eventual deed.

The track depends on the size and makeup of the estate. Florida has a no-administration option for very small personal-property estates, a summary route for modest ones, and full formal administration for the rest.

Which probate track fits an inherited house

The lightest track rarely reaches a house. Under s. 735.301, no administration is available only where what remains is exempt personal property and a limited amount of other personal property, so a home generally pushes the estate into summary or formal administration.

  • No administration: personal property only, with the court approving a transfer on an informal application.
  • Summary administration: open when the non-exempt estate is $150,000 or less, or when the owner has been dead more than 2 years (s. 735.201).
  • Formal administration: the standard route for larger estates, contested wills or a house that must be sold through a personal representative.

Thresholds can change, so confirm the current text with the probate clerk before you rely on one.

Notices the personal representative must send

The personal representative must promptly serve a notice of administration on the surviving spouse, the beneficiaries and anyone who may be entitled to exempt property (s. 733.212). Heirs under an older will can be served too.

That notice starts several clocks. An interested person who is served has 3 months from service to object to the will's validity, the venue or the court's jurisdiction. A person who may claim exempt property must petition by the later of 4 months after service or 40 days after related litigation ends. A surviving spouse who wants an elective share generally files by the earlier of 6 months after service or 2 years after the death, unless the court extends it.

Objections to validity, venue or jurisdiction are cut off no later than the earlier of the personal representative's final discharge or 1 year after service. Buyers and title companies often wait for the objection window to close before buying an estate house.

The notice gives the decedent's name, the file number, the court and its address, whether the estate is testate or intestate and, if there is a will, its date. It also names the personal representative and that person's attorney, so heirs know whom to contact about the house.

Creditor claim deadlines

A creditor must file a claim by the later of 3 months after the first publication of the notice to creditors or 30 days after being served, if that creditor had to be served (s. 733.702). Claims filed after that are barred.

Section 733.710 adds an outer limit. Two years after a person's death, the estate, the personal representative and the beneficiaries are no longer liable for claims against the decedent, except for a creditor who filed on time and has not been paid. A recorded mortgage or security interest is not wiped out by that limit, so the lender can still foreclose.

Estate tax and other costs

Florida has no estate tax. A federal change ended it for anyone who died after December 31, 2004, and since July 1, 2023 estates also skip Forms DR-312 and DR-313.

Inheriting a home can still create other costs. The county reassesses at just value after a change of ownership, which can lift a bill that was held down by the Save Our Homes cap.

Unpaid taxes while the estate is open

The tax calendar keeps running during a case. A tax certificate can be sold on an unpaid account after the delinquency date, and the collector can tell the personal representative what is owed and which payment months carry a discount. Keeping the account clear protects the title for a later buyer.

How probate affects the sale

The sale usually waits until the court issues authority to the personal representative, who then signs the deed. A deed signed by the estate representative is not subject to documentary stamp tax, unlike an ordinary sale between living owners.

After authority is in place, the family can list the house or sell it directly.

County offices that matter

Florida has 67 counties, and each elects its own clerk, property appraiser and tax collector. An estate with a house deals with all three, so the county of the property matters more than where the heirs live.

  • County clerk: handles the probate file, records the deed and collects documentary stamp tax at recording.
  • Property appraiser: sets just value each January 1 and decides whether a homestead exemption or other benefit applies.
  • Tax collector: sends the November bill, takes payment and sells tax certificates on unpaid accounts.

The deed that closes out the estate must meet the same form rules as any Florida conveyance, including two witnesses (s. 689.01). A title company reviewing an estate sale checks that detail alongside the court order.

What heirs should do before the house is sold

Start by locating the original will and asking the county clerk where it should be filed. Then plan around the property itself while the case runs.

  • Keep the property taxes and insurance current, since the bill keeps arriving whether or not title has moved.
  • Ask the property appraiser whether a homestead exemption was in place, because it ends when the owner no longer lives there as a permanent resident.
  • Ask the tax collector about the discount months and the delinquency date.
  • Wait on any contract until the personal representative has written authority.

Every county clerk runs its own probate division, and filing practices vary. Call the clerk before assuming that a form or fee from another county applies.

A cash buyer can close without a lender's timeline, which suits an estate that wants to stop carrying the house. The court's authority and the title company's checks still set the earliest closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Is probate unavoidable for an inherited house?

Often it is, when the dead owner held the house alone and no other transfer device applies. Real property falls outside the no-administration track meant for small personal-property estates. Ask the probate clerk or a Florida lawyer which track fits.

How much can an estate be worth to use summary administration?

The non-exempt estate may not exceed $150,000, or the decedent must have been dead more than 2 years (s. 735.201). Check the current wording with the clerk before relying on it.

What cutoff do creditors face?

They must file by the later of 3 months after first publication of the notice to creditors or 30 days after service, where service was required (s. 733.702). Two years after death, s. 733.710 cuts off most remaining claims against the estate.

Will the estate owe Florida estate tax?

No. Florida's estate tax ended for deaths after December 31, 2004, and Forms DR-312 and DR-313 have been unnecessary since July 1, 2023.

Does a deed from the estate carry stamp tax?

A deed from a personal representative under a probated will is not taxable. Estate-planning transfers in general have no specific exemption, so check other deeds with the clerk.
