Florida Homestead Protection: Devise Limits, Spouse Waivers and Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Florida
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Florida Homestead Protection: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Homestead Protection sale
  • Turn the Florida Homestead Protection offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Florida Homestead? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is and coordinate with the title company on spouse signatures.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Florida homestead is exempt from forced sale under court process, and it cannot be devised if the owner is survived by a spouse or minor child, with limited exceptions. A spouse who must join the deed has specific waiver language under Sec. 732.702.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

Protection from creditors

Article X, section 4 of the Florida Constitution puts a natural person's homestead out of reach of forced sale. No judgment, decree or execution becomes a lien on it. Three kinds of debt are carved out: taxes and assessments, money owed for buying, improving or repairing the property, and pay owed for labor on the realty.

Acreage limits depend on where the home sits. Outside a municipality the protected land can run to 160 contiguous acres. Inside a municipality the limit is one-half acre of contiguous land, and only the owner's residence or the owner's family residence is covered. Personal property up to $1,000 gets the same protection, and the shield carries over to a surviving spouse or heirs.

Leaving a homestead in a will

If the owner leaves a spouse or a minor child, the homestead cannot be devised freely. The Constitution blocks a devise in that situation, with one exception: it may go to the spouse when no minor child survives. Section 732.4015 repeats the rule.

A trust does not get around it. The statute treats a trust disposition of the part that would be homestead if titled in the grantor's own name as a devise, and the grantor of a qualifying trust is treated as the owner. When a spouse disclaims a devised interest, it passes under chapter 739.

Heirs planning a sale should know a will may not decide who holds title. Before insuring the sale, the closing agent will ask who survived the owner.

Who owns the house after a death with no valid devise

The home descends as intestate property, with special handling for spouses. When the owner leaves a spouse and descendants, the spouse receives a life estate and the descendants a vested remainder. Under s. 732.401 the spouse can trade that for an undivided one-half interest as a tenant in common, with the other half vesting in the descendants.

The trade follows strict steps:

  • It must happen within 6 months after death, and while the spouse is alive.
  • An attorney in fact or guardian needs court approval, and that petition also has to be filed inside the 6 months.
  • Once made, it cannot be undone.
  • The spouse records a notice of election, with the legal description, in the county's official records.

Until the election is made or the window closes, a buyer cannot tell what interest the spouse holds. If you are the seller, take the recorded notice, or proof that none was filed, to the title company early.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Spouse signature on the deed

A married owner of homestead land must have the spouse join in a sale. The Constitution says the owner, joined by the spouse if married, may transfer homestead by mortgage, sale or gift. A deed with only one spouse's signature leaves a gap that a title insurer will flag.

The same sentence allows a married owner to deed the property into a tenancy by the entirety with the spouse. If the owner or spouse is incompetent, transfer follows the method the law provides, which usually brings in a court or guardian.

Land conveyances also have to be written and signed before two subscribing witnesses under s. 689.01, so ask the closing agent to check the witness blocks.

What a spouse's waiver covers

It covers less than people assume. Section 732.7025 supplies deed language in which a spouse gives up the devise restriction, so the owner can leave the home to someone other than that spouse. Wording that is substantially similar to the statute's text is enough.

Two limits apply. The waiver leaves protection against the owner's creditors intact, during life or after death. It also leaves in place the rule that a spouse must join in any sale, mortgage or gift.

Section 732.702 is broader. A surviving spouse's rights to homestead, elective share, intestate share, family allowance and more can be waived in a written agreement signed before two subscribing witnesses. Waivers signed after marriage require fair disclosure of the signer's estate. In a property settlement, a waiver of "all rights" reaches homestead unless the document says otherwise.

Deed waiver versus written waiver

The two statutes do different jobs, and sellers often mix them up.

Point of comparisons. 732.7025 deed waivers. 732.702 written waiver
Where it appearsIn a deedStand-alone contract, agreement or waiver
ScopeDevise restriction onlyHomestead and other spousal rights, wholly or partly
WitnessesStatute prescribes the deed languageTwo subscribing witnesses
Effect on joinder to sellNone, joinder still requiredDepends on the waiver's terms

Have a lawyer draft or review either one.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling after probate or divorce

Both events can change who has to sign. After a death, work out whether the homestead passed by intestacy, whether a spouse made the six-month election, and whether the estate needs administration. Summary administration is available when the non-exempt estate does not exceed $150,000, or when the decedent has been dead more than two years (s. 735.201). Creditor claims are barred after the later of three months from first publication of the notice to creditors or 30 days after service on a creditor who must be served (s. 733.702).

Divorce runs on its own track. The constitutional joinder rule still governs any sale made before the court rules on the marital home, so the buyer's title agent will want the final judgment or the spouse's signature.

Documentary stamp tax rules apply as well. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is not taxable. Divorce deeds for the marital home, and spousal homestead deeds where the only consideration is a mortgage, are exempt under s. 201.02(7).

Documents to gather for the closing

Title work on a homestead rests on proof of who held title and who survived. Collect these before the contract goes out:

  • The death certificate and the deed that put the owner on title.
  • Any will or trust instrument, since a trust counts as a devise for homestead purposes.
  • A recorded notice of election, if a spouse chose the one-half interest.
  • Any marital agreement or waiver signed before two subscribing witnesses.
  • Divorce judgments that award the marital home.

The constitutional protection runs to heirs too. Creditors of the deceased owner face the same limits that applied during life, apart from the exceptions for taxes, purchase and improvement debts, and labor on the property.

A short call to the clerk of the circuit court tells you how recorded documents will appear in the official records. The clerk's recording charges are set by s. 28.24.

A cash buyer can close without waiting on a lender's underwriting, but the title company still needs every item above, so the paper chase is the same either way. Start it as soon as you decide to sell.

Frequently asked questions

Is a Florida homestead safe from judgment creditors?

Mostly. A court judgment cannot become a lien on it, though taxes, purchase or improvement debts and labor on the property are exceptions. The land limit is 160 acres outside a municipality and one-half acre inside one.

Can I leave my Florida homestead to my children if I am married?

Not by will or trust. With a surviving spouse, the home cannot go to someone else unless the spouse waived the restriction. A devise to the spouse works only if no minor child survives.

Does my wife or husband have to sign the deed to sell?

Yes, for a homestead. The Constitution calls for the spouse to join in a sale, mortgage or gift, and a deed without that signature can be challenged.

How long does a surviving spouse have to elect a half interest?

Six months from the date of death, and the spouse must still be living when the election is made. It cannot be revoked. The spouse records a notice of election with the clerk of that county.

Does the deed waiver language let me sell without my spouse?

No. Section 732.7025 waives only the devise restriction. Creditor protection and the spouse's joinder in a sale, mortgage or gift stay in place.

Florida Foreclosure Process: Judicial Sale, Redemption and Your Options

Cash Home Buyers in Florida

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Foreclosure Process sale

Facing Florida Foreclosure? Get a Cash Offer Before the Sale

A cash sale can pay your loan from the proceeds. Tell us your sale date and get a written offer.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling a house in Florida?

How foreclosure works in Florida

Florida foreclosures go through a court. The lender files suit, a judge enters a final judgment, and the circuit court clerk sells the home at a public sale. The owner can stop that sale at several points, and one of them is a sale of the house on the owner's own terms.

The process rests on Chapter 45 and Chapter 702 of the Florida Statutes. Chapter 45 covers the sale itself and the right to cure, and section 702.10 covers a faster path some lenders use through an order to show cause.

A homeowner served with a complaint should study every date on it and speak with a Florida attorney soon. Waiting seldom helps.

After the final judgment

The judgment directs the clerk to sell the property at public sale. Under section 45.031, the sale takes place not less than 20 days or more than 35 days after the judgment, unless the plaintiff agrees to a later date.

Notice goes out on a website under section 50.0311 for at least two consecutive weeks, or in a newspaper once a week for two consecutive weeks. The clerk may run the sale electronically.

  • The top bidder puts up 5 percent of the bid as a deposit.
  • The clerk files a certificate of sale.
  • If nobody objects within 10 days, the clerk files the certificate of title and the sale stands confirmed.

The winning bid counts as sufficient consideration, so a later argument about price faces a hard road.

Can you stop a Florida foreclosure sale?

Yes, up to a point. Section 45.0315 lets the mortgagor, or the holder of a subordinate interest, cure the debt and stop the sale at any time before the later of the clerk's filing of the certificate of sale or the time stated in the judgment.

The cure is paying the amount in the judgment. If no judgment exists yet, the owner tenders the performance due under the security agreement, including accelerated amounts, plus the lender's reasonable expenses of foreclosing, which include reasonable attorney's fees.

After that moment the door closes, and there is no right of redemption. A homeowner counting on a redemption period after the sale won't find one in this section.

The order to show cause route

Section 702.10 lets a lienholder ask for an order to show cause by filing a verified complaint. The hearing can be held no sooner than the later of 20 days after service of the order or 45 days after service of the complaint.

The resulting judgment operates against the property only, and a deficiency may still be allowed where the law permits it. Attorney fees up to 3 percent of principal need no reasonableness hearing.

One limit helps owners who live in the home. The payment or vacate order doesn't apply to owner occupied residences, and a granted homestead exemption on the latest tax roll is a rebuttable presumption that the home is owner occupied. Section 702.10 has the full text.

Foreclosure timing at a glance

Dates run from the judgment or the certificate of sale, so use the clerk's docket for the real calendar in your case.

Florida judicial foreclosure timing, sections 45.031, 45.0315 and 702.10
StepTiming
Sale after final judgmentNot less than 20 and not more than 35 days, unless the plaintiff consents to longer
Published notice of saleTwo consecutive weeks
Winning bidder deposit5 percent of the final bid
Objections after certificate of saleWithin 10 days
Show cause hearingNo sooner than the later of 20 days after the order is served or 45 days after the complaint reaches the owner
Right to cureUntil the later of the certificate of sale or the time set in the judgment

Surplus money after the sale

If the sale brings in more than the debt and costs, the extra is surplus funds. The final judgment has to carry a notice about them, and a homeowner is told to check with the clerk within 10 days after the sale.

Claims for surplus must be filed before the clerk reports the funds as unclaimed. Other lienholders may also claim a share, so look at the clerk's file before assuming anything is owed.

What to do when you get a foreclosure complaint

Read the summons for the response deadline and act inside it. A missed response can let the lender move toward judgment without your side being heard.

  • Collect the mortgage, note, payment history and any letters from the servicer.
  • Ask the circuit court clerk how to find your case on the docket.
  • Ask for the payoff in writing, since the cure under section 45.0315 depends on the amount in the judgment or the tender due.
  • Speak with a Florida attorney or a housing counselor before agreeing to anything.

Keeping a line open to the lender's attorney preserves choices, including a sale before the clerk fixes a date.

Taxes and recording costs

The certificate of title issued after a sale is a taxable document. Section 201.02(9) figures that tax on the highest and best bid at the sale.

Property taxes are separate. A change of ownership, a foreclosure included, resets the property to just value on the following January 1 for assessment, as the Department of Revenue's Save Our Homes guide explains. Owners who lose the home also lose the homestead exemption benefit, which is tied to permanent residence.

Selling before the auction

A sale on the open market or to a cash buyer pays off the lender from the money at the table, and the foreclosure case can then be dismissed. The deed in that sale carries the stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 in most counties, and every party to the deed is liable whichever side agrees to pay.

The target is the sale date the clerk has set. A buyer who can close ahead of it spares the owner an auction and leaves the owner in control of the price. If that's not possible, ask the lender's attorney whether the sale can be postponed. The plaintiff may consent to a date longer than 35 days.

Have the title agent confirm the payoff, junior liens and unpaid property tax before you sign a contract.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Your options before the sale date

An owner facing foreclosure has several paths, and each one affects timing and cost differently.

  • Cure the debt under section 45.0315 before the cutoff.
  • Sell the house before the sale, which pays the lender from the proceeds and avoids an auction.
  • Hand the lender a deed in lieu, a transfer the state revenue agency counts as a taxable deed.
  • Contest the case in court with an attorney's help.

Cash buyers often move quicker than a retail listing, which matters while the post judgment window is running. Call the clerk's office for the sale date, and get the lender's attorney to put the payoff in writing first.

Frequently asked questions

How long after judgment is a Florida foreclosure sale held?

The sale is set for not less than 20 days and not more than 35 days after the final judgment, unless the plaintiff agrees to a longer period.

Is there a redemption period after the sale in Florida?

No. Section 45.0315 gives a right to cure only until the later of the certificate of sale or the time in the judgment, and then closes the door on redemption.

Who runs the foreclosure sale?

The circuit court clerk. The clerk may conduct it electronically, publishes the notice, files the certificate of sale and later the certificate of title.

What is the deposit on a foreclosure bid?

The high bidder posts a deposit of 5 percent of the final bid, and objections are due within 10 days of the certificate.

Can I get surplus money after the sale?

Possibly. Surplus claims must be filed before the clerk reports the funds as unclaimed, and a homestead owner should check with the clerk within 10 days after the sale.

Florida Closing Costs: Doc Stamps, Title Insurance and Who Pays What

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Closing Costs sale

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling a house in Florida?

Closing costs a Florida seller faces

On the statute side, the big items are the stamp tax on the deed, the clerk's recording charges, title work and the seller's slice of the year's property tax. Commissions, repair credits and association fees come from the contract, not state law. Florida contracts leave much of this open, so the signed paper decides who pays each line.

This page covers the charges that a Florida statute or the Department of Revenue puts in writing. Ask your title agent or closing attorney to explain any other charge on the settlement sheet before you sign.

What the deed stamp tax comes to

The statutory rate is seventy cents for every $100 of consideration, counting any part of a hundred, in every county but Miami-Dade. Section 201.02 sets it. Consideration is a wide term: cash, a debt you're released from, and any mortgage or encumbrance on the parcel all count, whether or not the buyer assumes the loan.

Miami-Dade charges sixty cents per $100 plus a 45 cent surtax per $100. The surtax is skipped when the paper transfers only a single-family dwelling, so the clerk in that county can tell you which version fits your deed.

The clerk collects it at recording. A deed is taxable whether or not it's recorded, and a taxable paper that never gets recorded is paid to the Department itself. A certificate of title issued after a foreclosure sale is taxed on the highest and best bid under section 201.02(9).

Who pays the doc stamps?

Your contract names the payer, yet the state treats everyone on the document as liable. Liability stays with all parties whichever one agreed to pay, and a non-exempt party covers the tax when another party is exempt. No statute assigns the deed tax to a particular side.

If you agreed to pay, expect the title agent to subtract the tax from your proceeds at the table. These exemptions and exclusions apply:

  • Homestead deeds between spouses where the only consideration is a mortgage.
  • The deed that hands the marital home to one spouse in a divorce.
  • Estate deeds signed by a personal representative under a probated will, which the Department treats as not taxable.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Mortgage and note taxes

Mortgages and notes are taxed separately from the deed. The rate is 35 cents on each $100 secured, with the note tax capped at $2,450 and no cap on mortgages. These charges follow the buyer's financing, so an all-cash buyer owes none of them.

On your side, a lender holding your own mortgage wants payoff in full at closing. Order a written payoff statement a few days ahead, since interest accrues daily and the figure moves.

Clerk's recording fees

Under section 28.24, an instrument of ordinary size costs $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for every added page, with a $1.00 charge for each name past the fourth. A trust fund charge of $1.00 on page one and 50 cents on later pages sits on top, plus a $4 per page technology charge.

That adds up to far less than the stamp tax. A long deed with many grantors costs more than a short one, so have the closing agent quote the recording total before closing.

Does the seller pay for title insurance?

Whoever pays, the premium schedule comes from state rule. Florida's title insurance rate rule cites sections 627.782 and 627.7825 as its authority. Your contract names the party who buys the owner's policy, so read its title paragraph.

Section 627.7841 gives one protection worth knowing. If the insurer's own officers, employees or agents disburse your closing funds, the insurer must cover defects recorded after the commitment date and ahead of recording the deed, except those the insured knows about. That's a reason to close through a title agent who handles the money.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Signing the deed

Section 689.01 requires a deed for a freehold, or a lease running past one year, to be in writing with two subscribing witnesses. No seal is needed. Witnessing by audio-video technology is allowed, handy if you've already left the state.

Ask the title agent to send the deed for review before the closing date, so a missing witness or a misspelled name can't delay the closing.

Condo and HOA estoppel fees

A seller in an association community also orders an estoppel certificate. For a condominium, section 718.116 lets the association charge a reasonable fee of no more than $250 when nothing is delinquent, plus $100 for delivery within 3 business days and up to $150 more when money is owed. The homeowners' association statute, 720.30851, uses the same figures. Those caps are adjusted every five years. The Department of Business and Professional Regulation website shows today's amounts.

Our guide on selling a condo or HOA home covers the estoppel timeline and the documents a condo seller must hand over.

What to collect before closing

Gather the items that drive the final numbers and ask for each in writing.

  • Payoff letters from each lender or lienholder, dated near the closing.
  • An estoppel certificate if the home is in a condominium or homeowners' association.
  • The current tax bill from the tax collector, so the proration is checked against a real figure.
  • The proposed settlement statement a few days early, with the deed tax line matched to your contract price.
  • A copy of the recorded deed when the clerk sends it back.

A buyer planning to claim homestead must file with the appraiser's office by March 1, and a change of ownership resets the assessment to just value the following January 1. That reassessment is the buyer's concern, but it explains why buyers ask sellers for tax details.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Property taxes and listing disclosures

Tax bills arrive in November and carry an early-payment discount that steps down month by month until February. Anything still unpaid on April 1 is delinquent. The closing agent normally divides the annual bill with the buyer as the contract directs, and the tax collector can give you the current amount.

Residential buyers must receive a property tax disclosure at or before signing under section 689.261. It warns that the seller's present bill is a poor guide, because a sale or new improvements triggers reassessment. Starting February 1, 2027, listing materials may not show the current owner's tax amount, so ask your agent how your listing will read.

Florida sale charges at a glance
ChargeAmount
Deed stamp tax70 cents per $100 (Miami-Dade: 60 cents plus surtax)
Mortgage stamp tax35 cents per $100 secured
Note stamp tax limit$2,450
Recording, page one$5.00, plus $1.00 trust fund and $4 technology
Recording, later pages$4.00 each, plus 50 cents trust fund and $4 technology

Frequently asked questions

Who ends up paying the deed stamps?

The contract decides, but the state can collect from any party on the document. Read the closing cost paragraph of your contract for the agreed payer.

Will a cash buyer owe the mortgage tax?

No. That tax applies to mortgages and notes at 35 cents per $100 secured, and a cash purchase creates neither. That leaves the deed tax and recording charges.

Is Miami-Dade different?

Yes. The rate there is 60 cents per $100 plus a 45 cent surtax, and the surtax isn't due on a paper transferring only a single-family dwelling.

How much is recording a deed?

Under section 28.24 page one costs $5.00 and added pages cost $4.00 each, with a trust fund charge, a $4 per page technology charge and $1.00 per name past four.

When do property tax bills come and go delinquent?

Bills are mailed in November, and unpaid ones become delinquent on April 1. The closing agent splits the year's bill between you and the buyer.

Disclosures a Florida seller must give

A seller of Florida residential property owes the buyer three statutory notices: a flood disclosure, a property tax summary and a radon notice. An agent also has a duty to reveal known hidden defects that affect value.

Each notice has its own deadline, tied to the moment the contract is signed. Giving one late, or leaving one out, invites a dispute at closing. The sections below take them in the order they usually come up.

The flood disclosure

The seller completes a flood disclosure and gives it to the buyer at or before the time the sales contract is signed. The statute prints the form, which opens with a warning that homeowners' insurance policies do not include coverage for flood damage and urges the buyer to ask an insurance agent about separate flood coverage.

You then answer three checkbox questions:

  • whether you know of any flooding that damaged the property while you owned it;
  • whether you have filed an insurance claim for flood damage, including a claim under the National Flood Insurance Program;
  • whether you have received assistance for flood damage, including assistance from FEMA.

The form defines flooding as a general or temporary condition of partial or complete inundation. It names three causes: overflow of inland or tidal waters, unusual and rapid buildup of runoff or surface water from a source such as a river, stream or drainage ditch, and sustained standing water after rainfall.

Answer from your own records. If you cannot recall whether a claim was filed, check old insurance correspondence before you tick a box.

The property tax disclosure summary

The buyer must receive a property tax disclosure summary at or before signing, either built into the contract or attached to it. Unless the contract includes it, the seller must provide it.

Its message is simple: the buyer should not treat your current property taxes as the amount owed next year, because a change of ownership or new improvements trigger reassessment. Questions about valuation go to the county property appraiser.

If the summary is a separate document, the contract must refer to it and carry prominent language telling the buyer not to sign until the summary has been read. That reference is easy to overlook in a homemade contract.

Property tax listings in 2027

Starting February 1, 2027, a home shown on a public listing platform must carry an estimated ad valorem tax figure in place of the current owner's bill. The same date bars the current owner's taxes from printed listing materials.

The platform may estimate by applying current millage rates to the listing price, using a formula the Department of Revenue publishes, or using the countywide average millage rate. Either way it must add a disclaimer that millage varies within a county and that the estimate leaves out non-ad valorem assessments, exemptions and the transfer of a homestead assessment difference. The Department of Revenue is to publish the formula and rate data from December 15, 2026, and every year after. No cause of action arises against anyone for an inaccurate estimate.

For you, that means listing photos and copy should not quote your own tax bill. Ask your agent how the platform will show the estimate.

The radon notice

Florida requires a radon notice on at least one document signed at or before a contract for sale of any building. Standard contract forms normally carry it already.

The required text describes radon as a naturally occurring radioactive gas that can present health risks over time when it builds up in a building. It adds that levels above federal and state guidelines have been found in Florida buildings, and that the county health department can supply information on radon and testing. Transient occupancy of 45 days or less is excluded.

Anyone who measures or mitigates radon for a fee must be certified by the state, so ask for a certification number if a buyer orders a test.

What you must reveal beyond the forms

An agent working with a seller must disclose all known facts that materially affect the value of residential property and are not readily observable to the buyer. That duty applies to single agents, transaction brokers and agents with no brokerage relationship alike.

Florida also draws a line on stigma. The fact that a property was, or was suspected to have been, the site of a homicide, suicide or death is not a material fact that must be disclosed. The same holds for an occupant's HIV infection or AIDS diagnosis, and no cause of action arises against an owner or agent for staying silent on either.

When each item is due
DisclosureTiming or status
Flood disclosureAt or before contract execution
Property tax summaryAt or before contract execution
Radon noticeOn at least one document at or before contract
Death on the propertyNot a required disclosure

A known defect that affects value and that a buyer could not readily see falls under the agent's duty above, so tell your agent about it and put it in writing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How property taxes reset after the sale

The buyer's tax bill can differ sharply from yours, which is the reason for the tax summary. A sale, foreclosure or other change of legal or beneficial title resets the property to just value the following January 1, with exceptions such as transfers between spouses.

The annual calendar runs like this:

  • January 1 is the assessment date.
  • March 1 is the filing deadline for exemptions and classifications with the property appraiser.
  • In August the appraiser mails the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes, and a value challenge petition is due 25 days after that notice.
  • In November the tax collector sends bills, with early-payment discounts of 4 percent in November, 3 percent in December, 2 percent in January and 1 percent in February.
  • Unpaid taxes become delinquent on April 1.

Ask the county tax collector for the status of the current bill before you list, since unpaid taxes come out of your proceeds.

Selling as-is and your disclosure duties

Selling as-is changes the price conversation, not the paperwork. The three notices still go to the buyer, and a known defect that a buyer could not readily see still has to be shared through your agent. Gather your insurance and claim records, your tax bill and any repair estimates before the contract is drafted, so the forms get filled in once and correctly. A cash buyer who takes the house in its current condition will still receive the same notices.

A simple order of work helps. Fill in the flood answers from your own records first. Confirm the tax summary is attached to or built into the contract. Check that the radon notice appears on a document the buyer signs. Then call the tax collector for the bill status so nothing surprises you at the closing table.

Frequently asked questions

When must I give the buyer the flood disclosure?

At or before the time the sales contract is signed. The statute sets that deadline and prints the form.

Do I have to tell a buyer someone died in the house?

No. A death, homicide or suicide on the property is not a material fact that must be disclosed, and no lawsuit arises from staying silent.

Can I advertise my current property tax bill on a listing?

Not after February 1, 2027. From that date the current owner's ad valorem taxes cannot appear in printed listing materials, and listing platforms must show an estimate instead.

Is a radon notice required if my home tested low?

Yes. The notice goes on at least one document signed at or before the contract and does not depend on a test result.

Does an as-is sale remove disclosure duties?

No. The statutory notices apply to a residential sale whatever the condition, and an agent still must disclose known material facts that the buyer cannot readily observe.

A Florida owner who sells their own property does not need a real estate license, but still has to give the buyer required disclosures and sign a properly witnessed deed. This guide uses Chapter 475 and the disclosure statutes.

Can I sell my house without an agent in Florida?

Yes. Florida places no licensing requirement on an owner who sells their own home. Several written disclosures and recording rules still land on the seller, though.

The paperwork falls into three groups: what the buyer must receive before signing the contract, what the deed must look like, and what the tax and county offices need afterward. The sections below follow that order.

Disclosures a Florida seller must hand over

Two statutory forms apply to residential sales: a property tax disclosure summary and a flood disclosure. The buyer needs each one no later than contract signing.

Written items a Florida seller gives the buyer
DisclosureStatuteWhat it covers
Property tax disclosure summarys. 689.261Warns the buyer not to assume the seller's tax bill carries over, since a change of ownership or improvements can trigger reassessment
Flood disclosures. 689.302Seller's knowledge of past flooding, any flood insurance claim, and any flood assistance received

If the tax summary is not built into the contract, it must be attached. The contract then has to refer to it and tell the buyer not to sign until it has been read.

What the flood disclosure asks

The form opens with a notice that homeowners' policies do not cover flood damage and that the buyer should talk to an insurance agent about separate flood coverage. After that it asks three things:

  • Any flood damage you know of while you owned the home.
  • Whether you filed a flood damage claim, including with the National Flood Insurance Program.
  • Whether you received help for flood damage, including from FEMA.

The statute defines flooding as inundation from overflowing inland or tidal water, rapid runoff from an established water source such as a ditch, or sustained standing water after rainfall.

Listing rules on property taxes from 2027

Beginning February 1, 2027, online listings must display a tax estimate, and printed marketing must drop the owner's present tax figure.

Section 689.261(3) builds the estimate from the listing price at current millage rates, or from the countywide average rate, using data the Department of Revenue publishes. No one is liable for an inaccurate estimate. In practice, leave your own tax amount off flyers, and expect online listings to lean on the estimator.

The deed and closing paperwork

The deed is a written instrument signed before two subscribing witnesses (s. 689.01). To be recorded under s. 695.26 it needs printed names, addresses and blank margin space for the clerk.

  • A warranty deed or another deed type that matches what you promise the buyer.
  • Printed names and post-office addresses for signers, witnesses and the preparer.
  • Stamp tax paid when the deed is recorded, at the statewide deed rate (Miami-Dade has its own schedule).
  • Clerk recording charges that depend on page count.

Every party stays liable for the stamp tax, so the contract should say who pays. If you would rather not handle a deed alone, a title company or attorney can run the closing.

How a sale affects your tax bill and exemption

Bills go to whoever owns the property of record, so the settlement statement is where a year's tax gets divided.

Paying early in November earns the biggest state-printed discount, and the discount steps down each month to 1 percent in February. Assessment returns to just value after a sale, so the buyer's bill may look nothing like yours. The buyer files a fresh homestead application. You should tell the property appraiser you sold so your own exemption is cancelled.

Tax lien risks when there is no closing agent

A sale does not erase an unpaid tax bill. A private seller should confirm the year's taxes are paid or credited at closing.

Taxes turn delinquent on April 1, and certificates on unpaid parcels are auctioned by June 1. A certificate holder waits two years before pressing the owner, and a tax deed application may follow. On a homestead, a tax deed sale opens at the amounts due plus half the latest assessed value (ss. 197.432 and 197.502). Keep the account current through closing.

Order of steps in a private sale

Work backward from the closing date, since several steps can only start once an earlier one is done.

  • Order a title search and clear any liens before the house is listed.
  • Prepare the property tax summary and the flood disclosure so they can go out with the contract.
  • Put in the contract who bears the deed tax and recording fees.
  • Prepare the deed, then sign it before two witnesses and a notary.
  • File the signed deed with the county clerk along with the stamp tax.
  • Notify the property appraiser of the sale and cancel your exemptions.

Property tax dates sellers should know

The state calendar is the same for every Florida seller.

  • January 1: the appraiser sets just value.
  • March 1: last timely day to apply for exemptions.
  • August: the TRIM notice arrives, and a value petition is due within 25 days.
  • November: tax bills go out.
  • April 1: unpaid taxes turn delinquent.

Whatever the closing date, set the proration in the contract and ask the county tax collector for a payoff figure.

Should a seller order a title search?

Yes, and early. A buyer's lender will want clear title. A search turns up liens, prior deeds and the exact names that must appear on the new deed. It also shows whether the owner of record matches the people who will sign, which spares you a rejected recording at the clerk's counter.

It is also the moment to catch an old homestead exemption you forgot to cancel, or a tax account carrying a deferral. Both change the closing figures.

Payment plans and deferrals

You may have one, though a sale changes things. A homestead tax deferral is requested on Form DR-570 by March 31 after the assessment year, and it covers taxes above 5 percent of household income. Installment prepayment must be requested by May 1 of the assessment year under s. 197.222, and partial payments are at the collector's discretion before the delinquency date.

Deferred or installment balances come out of the closing proceeds, so ask the tax collector for a written payoff before the closing date.

Other risks FSBO sellers overlook

Three come up often: lender liens, county tax liens and occupants.

  • Delinquent taxes lead down a path to a certificate sale, so settle the bill.
  • Occupants need proper notice before closing; section 83.57 sets 30 days for a month-to-month tenancy.
  • A buyer's lender will want clear title, so order the title search early.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record the deed after a private sale?

With the clerk of the circuit court in the county where the land sits. The clerk records documents and collects stamp tax, so bring a deed that follows the printed-name and margin rules.

Is a lawyer required for a private sale?

No statute requires one. A Florida attorney or title company can prepare the deed, check title and handle recording, and many sellers hire one for the closing even when they find their own buyer.

Must a FSBO seller give a property tax disclosure?

Yes. Section 689.261 requires the buyer to receive the summary at or before signing the contract. It can sit inside the contract or ride along as a separate attachment.

Is the flood disclosure required even if my house never flooded?

Yes. The form still goes to the buyer, and you mark that you know of no flooding, no claim and no assistance. It is due at or before contract signing under s. 689.302.

May I put my present tax bill in a flyer?

After February 1, 2027, no. Printed marketing must leave out the owner's current ad valorem taxes, and online platforms must use estimators. The appraiser's website has an estimator.

The Florida property tax year

Each tax year in Florida starts from one fixed date: your county property appraiser sets just value on every parcel as of January 1. What follows is a predictable sequence, laid out below, ending with a bill from the tax collector.

Dates to mark on your calendar
WhenWhat happens
January 1Parcels valued at just value
March 1Last day to file for exemptions or special classifications
April 1Business owners file the DR-405 for tangible personal property
AugustTRIM notice (DR-474) goes out
Sept. to Nov.Tentative and final budget and millage hearings
NovemberBills (DR-528) mailed

Two clocks matter here. Disagree with the value and you have 25 days from the TRIM notice to petition; get an exemption denied and the window is 30 days from the denial letter.

Early payment discounts

Paying early saves money. November payers get 4 percent off, and the cut shrinks by a point with each passing month until it reaches 1 percent in February. After that you owe the full amount.

Once April 1 arrives with nothing paid, the account is delinquent. Certificates against the unpaid balance are sold by June 1, so waiting past April costs you control of the timeline.

Homestead exemption

Your assessment can shrink by up to $50,000 with a homestead exemption. Think of it as two slices. Slice one is $25,000 and counts against all levies, school taxes among them. Slice two is up to $25,000 more, but it only bites on assessed value past the $50,000 mark and school taxes ignore it. Slice two moves with CPI each January 1 when CPI is up, and holds steady when CPI is down.

  • The home must be your permanent residence as of January 1.
  • Form DR-501 goes to the appraiser by March 1.
  • Renting the place, moving out or leaving the state ends the benefit.
  • Servicemembers may rent a homestead without losing it.

Save Our Homes cap

Year one on a homestead is at full just value. After that the Save Our Homes cap limits growth: the yearly increase in assessed value is held to 3 percent or the CPI change, whichever is lower, and assessed value stays at or under just value. A cap chart revised January 2026 sits on the Department of Revenue site.

Non-homestead parcels have a 10 percent yearly limit instead. When ownership changes, both limits fall away. A sale, a foreclosure or any shift in legal or beneficial title counts as a change.

Portability: moving your cap

Buying another Florida home does not have to wipe out your cap savings. Whatever gap built up on the old home can lower the new home's assessment, to a maximum of $500,000. The catch is timing: the new homestead has to be in place within three years, counting from January 1 of the year the old homestead ended.

Send DR-501T along with DR-501 by March 1. Amendments passed recently start applying with the 2027 roll, so ring the appraiser to check the limits in force.

TRIM notice and November bill

Think of the August TRIM notice as a preview, never a demand for payment. You will see prior and current values, the millage each taxing body is asking for, and the hearing dates. November's bill shows the final numbers after the hearings.

  • Compare three figures: just value, assessed value and taxable value. A homestead often shows assessed value under just value.
  • Find your exemption on the notice. When it is absent, see the appraiser quickly, because a denial notice starts a 30-day window.
  • Scan the line for each taxing body (county, school board, city) and compare it with last year's.
  • If you think value is off, you have 25 days from the notice to petition.

When a sale or refinance is coming, request your parcel's payoff figure from the tax collector. The amount moves as the discount changes each month.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Benefits for older owners and servicemembers

Most of these benefits depend on local ordinance, so your county and city decide what you get.

  • Age 65 or older: your local government may add up to $50,000 if household income falls under its cap.
  • Seniors with a permanent disability from service: a discount matching the VA rating.
  • Ex-servicemembers discharged honorably with a 10 percent or higher rating: $5,000 comes off assessed value.
  • Deployed servicemembers: a proportional exemption, filed on Form DR-501M.

Deferral works separately. Before March 31, ask the tax collector about Form DR-570 and the income thresholds your household would face.

Who sets the rate?

Every taxing body on your bill sets its millage at fall hearings. The tentative budget hearing falls in September or October, and the final one in October or November. State law ties growth in a taxing body's property tax revenue to growth in Florida per capita personal income plus new construction, unless a super-majority, unanimous vote or referendum goes beyond that.

The TRIM notice prints proposed millage, which makes August the time to plan on attending one.

Installments and deferral

Installment prepayment starts with an application filed at the tax collector's office on or before May 1 of the assessment year. Partial payments ahead of delinquency are the collector's call.

Ask which version your county runs. Installments and homestead deferral are different programs with different filing dates.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What a delinquent account can lead to

Bidders compete on interest, and the collector gives each certificate to the lowest rate offered, in quarter-point increments. The certificate holder cannot press the owner for 2 years, measured from April 1 of the issuance year. A tax deed application may come after that.

The clerk then runs the public auction. Homestead parcels open higher than other property, because half of the latest assessed value gets added to what is owed. Pay before a certificate exists if you can, since every step after that adds cost.

What buyers and heirs should check

Do not use a seller's bill as a forecast of yours. Someone who has owned a homestead for years may be assessed far below just value because of the cap, and that gap closes at transfer.

  • What is the parcel's just value compared with its assessed value?
  • Is the current exemption tied to the seller's residence, and will it end at closing?
  • Are any tax certificates outstanding on the parcel?
  • Which taxing bodies levy on this address, and did any propose higher millage?

Both offices will answer by phone or at the counter, and those answers let you budget before you offer on a house or take one over.

Selling before taxes are paid

At closing, the title company divides that year's taxes between you and the buyer. Beforehand, ask the collector for the current balance and for any certificate on the parcel. The appraiser can explain what your sale does to the exemption.

Plan on the next owner paying a good deal more than you did. The parcel returns to just value on the January 1 after the sale, no matter how the buyer pays. Back taxes come out of what you receive, so get that payoff amount in writing.

Frequently asked questions

When does Florida mail property tax bills?

In November, from the county tax collector. The early discount runs 4 percent in November down to 1 percent in February.

Which date makes Florida taxes delinquent?

April 1. Certificates on unpaid accounts are sold by June 1.

Which form claims a homestead exemption?

Form DR-501, filed with the county property appraiser by March 1. You must have made the home your permanent residence by January 1.

What is the annual growth limit on homestead value?

The smaller of 3 percent or the CPI change. The Department of Revenue chart shows 2.7 percent for 2026.

How does deferral work for homestead owners?

File DR-570 with the tax collector by March 31 after the assessment year. It covers taxes above 5 percent of household income, or above 3 percent for a permanent resident 65 or older.

A Florida owner who has legal or beneficial title on January 1 and makes the property a permanent residence is entitled to the homestead exemption, and must apply with the county property appraiser by March 1. A change of ownership ends the Save Our Homes cap.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

What the exemption is worth

The Florida homestead exemption takes up to $50,000 off the assessed value of your home before tax is figured. It comes in two layers. Layer one is $25,000 and hits every levy, schools too. Layer two is another $25,000, but it only covers assessed value over $50,000 and never touches school taxes.

The second layer moves with inflation. When the CPI change is positive, the amount is adjusted each January 1. When it is negative, the amount holds steady. The state's table starts from a 2024 base, so read your own bill or phone the appraiser for the figure now in force.

All it does is shrink the taxable base. Each taxing district's millage still applies to the value that remains.

Who qualifies and what ends it

To qualify you hold title on January 1 and also live there as a permanent resident by that date. One permanent residence per owner.

Three things end it:

  • You rent the home out.
  • The house stops being your permanent home.
  • You stop being a Florida permanent resident.

Servicemembers have an exception under s. 196.061 that lets them lease the home without giving up homestead. Anyone else who moves away should tell the appraiser, so an exemption you no longer qualify for does not stay on the roll.

How to apply, and what to do if you are denied

Send Form DR-501 to your county property appraiser. Exemption and agricultural classification claims close on March 1.

After a denial letter arrives, the value adjustment board petition is due in 30 days. Arguing about value is another track altogether. That petition is Form DR-486, filed with the clerk of court within 25 days of the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes mailed in August.

Eligibility is the appraiser's call. Bills come from the tax collector. When a problem could belong to either, call the appraiser first.

Save Our Homes cap

Save Our Homes slows the yearly climb in a homestead's assessed value. Past year one, the rise is held to 3 percent or the CPI change, whichever is smaller, and assessed value can never pass just value.

YearCPI changeCap applied
20243.4%3.0%
20252.9%2.9%
20262.7%2.7%

The 2024 row shows the 3 percent ceiling biting while inflation ran higher. Property without homestead faces a ceiling of 10 percent per year.

What happens to the cap when you sell

Whatever protection you built up is gone once the house sells. Foreclosure, or passing legal or beneficial title in any other way, is also a change of ownership. On the next January 1 the assessor resets the parcel to just value. Transfers between spouses and certain transfers at death are carved out.

The exemption does not travel either. A buyer who moves in files a new claim, and one who rents it out cannot claim at all. After many years of ownership, the new owner's first full bill can run far above yours.

A closing in spring or summer still falls in a tax year whose assessment was fixed the previous January, and the November bill is split under the purchase contract. Read that clause before you sign.

Moving the savings to another house

If you buy again in Florida, portability can carry over your Save Our Homes savings, but a deadline applies. The new homestead has to be established within three years. Counting starts on January 1 of the year you abandoned the old homestead, and closing day is irrelevant. Form DR-501T goes in with the DR-501.

Under s. 193.155(8), the new home's assessed value drops by the smaller of $500,000 and the old home's just-minus-assessed difference. Changes made by ch. 2026-239 start with the 2027 roll, so confirm with the appraiser which rules cover your move.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Extra breaks for seniors, service members and disabled owners

More relief can stack on the base exemption. Some of it depends on a local vote.

  • Age 65 and up: a county or city may pass an ordinance adding up to $50,000, but only for households under an income cap. The cap started at $20,000 and moves with CPI (s. 196.075(2)).
  • Longtime seniors (65 plus, 25 years as a permanent resident, just value under $250,000): an ordinance can wipe out the whole assessed value if income qualifies.
  • Military retirees 65 and older with a permanent service-connected disability: a discount equal to the VA disability percentage, which an unremarried surviving spouse keeps (s. 196.082).
  • Former servicemembers with a disability rating of 10 percent or more: $5,000 off assessed value (ss. 196.081, 196.091).
  • Total and permanent service-connected disability: the homestead may be fully exempt.

Your appraiser can tell you which ones your county offers.

Deferring homestead tax

Some homeowners postpone part of the bill instead of paying it. The paperwork is Form DR-570, and the tax collector must have it by March 31 following the assessment year. The deferrable amount is the part above 5 percent of last year's household income, or the whole bill if income is under $10,000. Owners 65 and older who are permanent residents can defer the part above 3 percent of income.

If you pay on time, the early-payment discount is largest in November at 4 percent and falls each month: 3 percent for December, 2 for January, 1 for February. Anything unpaid is delinquent from April 1, and the county sells tax certificates by June 1.

Before you list, get a payoff number from the tax collector. The deferred amount comes out of your sale proceeds at the closing table, and the title company needs the figure to clear it.

Checklist before you list a homestead

Start with the parcel record on the appraiser's site, which lists assessed value, just value and exemption status. The distance between the two values is what Save Our Homes has kept off your bill.

  • Confirm your current exemption application was accepted.
  • Note any senior, veteran or disability benefit. None of them transfers to a buyer.
  • Find out whether a DR-570 deferral is on record.
  • Decide early whether you plan to port the benefit, because that starts a three year window.

Hand your answers to the closing agent so the buyer can plan a new filing. Ask your agent or title company to build the property tax proration around the numbers on the parcel record, not around an estimate.

Pull your last two tax bills as well. Compare the line for each taxing body, since school, county and city rates differ, and a buyer's agent will probably do the same. Seeing which levies the exemption actually reduces shows whether the buyer's real cost after reassessment will be close to yours or far above it. If you remodeled recently, ask the appraiser whether the new improvements were added to the roll, because additions can raise just value on their own.

A cash buyer skips the lender's escrow setup and appraisal timeline, but the reassessment still happens the following January 1 either way.

Frequently asked questions

When must a Florida homestead claim be filed?

Your county appraiser needs Form DR-501 by March 1. Residency matters too: the house must already be your permanent home on January 1. A rejected claim can be taken to the value adjustment board, and the clock there is 30 days.

How big is the Florida homestead exemption?

Think of it as two slices. The first $25,000 reduces every tax bill line. The next $25,000 only helps once assessed value passes $50,000, skips the school line, and grows with inflation.

Does a buyer inherit my Save Our Homes cap?

No. When the deed changes hands, the new owner starts at full just value from the next January 1. Spouses and certain death transfers get different treatment.

Can I keep my cap savings when I buy elsewhere in Florida?

Portability may let you. Set up the next homestead inside the three year window that begins on January 1 of the year you left the old one, and send DR-501T with the DR-501. Your benefit is capped at $500,000 or at the old home's just-minus-assessed difference, whichever is smaller.

What if I rent my homestead out?

Then you lose it. Leasing the home, moving out, or giving up Florida permanent residency each end the exemption. Servicemembers have a carve-out in s. 196.061.

Selling a house in Florida?

How to appeal your assessment

You start by filing a sworn petition with the clerk of your county's value adjustment board, called the VAB. The petition is due within 25 days of the date the property appraiser mailed your Notice of Proposed Property Taxes. That notice is the TRIM notice, and it goes out in August.

You can talk with the appraiser's office first, but an informal conference is not required before a petition, and the 25-day clock keeps running while you talk. Filing the petition is the safer way to hold your place.

Deadlines for a VAB petition

Which deadline you face depends on what you dispute. A valuation complaint must be filed on or before the 25th day after the notice is mailed. A denied exemption, a denied agricultural or high-water recharge classification, a denied historic-property classification or a denied deferral gets 30 days after the mailing of the notice that carries the denial.

  • Valuation dispute: 25 days from the mailed TRIM notice.
  • Exemption, classification or deferral denial: 30 days from the denial notice.
  • Hearing evidence: lists and copies exchanged at least 15 days before the hearing.
  • Written board decision: due within 20 calendar days after the board's last session.
  • Circuit court suit: 60 days from certification of the assessment, or from the board decision in the cases the statute describes.

Who can file or represent you

You can file as the owner, or you can authorize someone to file for you. The petition needs your signature or a written authorization or power of attorney, and an authorization covers only one assessment year. A person who appears for you can be an employee of yours, a Florida Bar attorney, a real estate appraiser or broker with a license, a certified public accountant you retain, or an unpaid person holding your written authorization.

The petition names the property by parcel number and says about how much time you expect to need. The property appraiser can use an attorney too, and witnesses on both sides testify under oath if either party asks.

What happens at the VAB hearing?

The board hears you and the property appraiser, and each side can cross-examine witnesses under Department of Revenue rules. At least 15 days before the hearing you hand the appraiser your list of evidence, copies of documents and a summary of witness testimony. The appraiser owes you the same, including the property record card. If the appraiser skips that duty, the hearing is rescheduled.

The board can look at assessments of comparable properties in similar areas. It cannot consider evidence the appraiser asked you for in writing and you held back. A verbatim record of the hearing is kept.

What to gather before you file

Pull together the TRIM notice, the parcel number and the property record card, which the appraiser must give you before the hearing. Comparable properties in your neighborhood carry the most weight, since the board can weigh assessments among comparable properties in similar areas.

  • The mailing date printed on the TRIM notice, so you can count 25 days.
  • Photos or repair estimates if the home's condition is the issue.
  • Recent sales of similar homes nearby.
  • A signed authorization if someone else files for you.

Ask the VAB clerk in your county for the Department of Revenue petition form and the local way to submit it, because counties differ. The petition is sworn and goes to the clerk, who acknowledges receipt and passes a copy to the appraiser. A county officer cannot turn away the department's form if you choose to use it. Keep your acknowledgment, since it proves you met the deadline.

The board's decision and what comes next

Unless the petition is withdrawn or the appraiser agrees with you, the board issues a written decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law within 20 calendar days after its last session. The clerk mails the result to you and the appraiser, or sends it electronically if you chose that on the petition.

Florida appeal steps and their time limits
StepTime limit
File with the VAB clerk25 days after the notice for value, 30 days after a denial notice for an exemption or classification
Exchange evidenceAt least 15 days before the hearing
Board decisionWithin 20 calendar days after the last session
Circuit court action60 days after certification or the board decision

If you still disagree, circuit courts have original jurisdiction over property tax disputes, with venue in the property's county in most cases. Keep your copy of the decision, because the 60-day court limit can run from the board's ruling.

Paying while you contest in court

Before you sue, you must pay the tax collector at least the tax you admit in good faith that you owe, and file the receipt with your complaint. Paying does not concede that the tax was right, and a timely suit pauses collection until the case ends.

Taxes on the same property for later years, to the extent you admit them, have to be paid before they turn delinquent. If you miss that, the court loses jurisdiction. These payment rules are jurisdictional, so a missing receipt can end the case.

Joint appeals by neighbors or associations

Sometimes a group can file together. A condominium, cooperative or homeowners' association with board approval may file one joint petition for owners whose units the appraiser finds substantially similar in location, amenities, rooms, living area and condition. The association has to notify owners first and give them at least 14 days to opt out in writing.

An owner of contiguous undeveloped parcels, or of several tangible personal property accounts, can also seek a joint petition if the appraiser finds them substantially similar. A business personal property assessment cannot be contested unless the required return was filed on time.

Homestead portability disputes

If you moved a homestead and disagree with the assessment difference carried over, you petition in the county of the new home. That board notifies the board in the old county, which reconvenes if needed. You cannot use this proceeding to change the old home's just, assessed or taxable value.

Portability itself requires you to establish the new homestead within three years of January 1 of the year you abandoned the old one, with Form DR-501T filed alongside the DR-501 by March 1.

If you plan to sell while the appeal is open

An open appeal does not stop you from selling, but tell the closing agent and the title company about it early. Ask the tax collector for the current balance and whether any part of the bill is under dispute. The price a buyer pays also resets the property to just value the following January 1, so a lower assessment this year may not follow the house to the next owner. A buyer paying cash for the home in its current condition can close without waiting on the board.

Frequently asked questions

What is the deadline to appeal my Florida property value?

File with the VAB clerk by the 25th day after the property appraiser mails the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes. A denied exemption, classification or deferral carries a 30-day window from the denial notice.

Do I need to meet with the property appraiser first?

No. You can ask for an informal conference, but it is not a prerequisite to a petition or a lawsuit. The petition deadline keeps running while you talk.

Can I hire someone to file for me?

Yes. An attorney, a real estate appraiser or broker with a license, a CPA, an employee of yours or a person with written authorization or a power of attorney can act for you. The authorization is good for one assessment year and one petitioner.

How long does the board have to decide?

The board must issue its written decision within 20 calendar days after its last day in session. The clerk then sends notice to you and the property appraiser.

Can I sue in circuit court instead?

You can contest an assessment in circuit court whether or not you filed with the board, but you must pay the tax you admit owing first. The suit must come within 60 days of the dates the statute names.

Florida Tax Deed Sales: Certificates, Redemption and Surplus Funds

Cash Home Buyers in Florida
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Tax Deed Sales sale
  • Turn the Florida Tax Deed Sales offer down and you owe us nothing

Behind on Taxes? Get a Cash Offer Before a Tax Sale

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling a house in Florida?

How a Florida tax deed sale starts

It starts with unpaid property tax. The tax collector mails bills in November, taxes turn delinquent on April 1, and the tax collector sells tax certificates on unpaid items by June 1.

A certificate is not a deed. It is a lien the buyer purchases by bidding, and the house stays in the owner's name until a deed is issued after a longer process. An owner who is behind has real time to act.

How tax certificates are sold

Bidders compete on interest, and the lowest rate wins. The tax collector awards each certificate to the bidder who demands the lowest rate, in quarter percent steps, and unsold certificates go to the county at the maximum rate.

  • A homestead property with less than $250 delinquent must be issued to the county, not sold at auction.
  • The tax collector keeps a 5 percent commission.
  • The holder may not contact the owner to demand payment until two years after the April 1 that falls in the year of issuance.

Can you pay off a certificate and keep the house?

Yes, at any time after issuance and before a tax deed is issued, as long as the buyer has not yet paid in full for the deed. You pay the tax collector the face amount plus interest, costs and charges.

When the certificate's earned interest is below 5 percent of face value, a mandatory minimum of 5 percent applies, except on certificates bid at zero percent. The tax collector receives a $6.25 fee per redeemed certificate. A certificate can also be redeemed in part only when the portion can be identified by legal description and is backed by a sale contract or recorded deed. Call the collector for the exact payoff figure on your parcel.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

When the holder can apply for a tax deed

The holder can apply once two years go by from the April 1 that falls in the year the certificate was issued. The application fee is $75, and the tax collector lists the people who must receive notice: the titleholder, lienholders, mortgagees, contract for deed buyers and the assessed party.

Notice goes to a defined group, so an updated mailing address with the property appraiser and the clerk helps. The clerk's own charge for processing a tax deed application is $60.00.

What the opening bid includes

It includes the taxes, interest and costs owed, and for homestead property it also adds one half of the latest assessed value. That is a notable difference from a non-homestead parcel.

If nobody bids, the land goes on the list of lands available for taxes. The county then has 90 days to buy it for the opening bid. Three years after the offer, remaining land escheats to the county.

How the clerk runs the sale and collects payment

The circuit court clerk holds the public auction, and electronic sales are allowed.

  • The high bidder pays a nonrefundable deposit of 5 percent of the bid or $200, whichever is greater.
  • Full payment, documentary stamps and recording fees are due within 24 hours, excluding weekends and holidays.
  • The certificate holder's bid also earns interest at a monthly rate of 1.5 percent.

To stop the sale, redeem before the winning bidder pays for the deed. After that, the remedy shifts to surplus funds.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Surplus after a tax deed sale

Whatever the winning bid exceeds the certificate holder's statutory bid goes into a surplus, and lienholders are paid first.

The clerk pays governmental liens of record first, then holds the balance for the people with an interest in the property and mails them a notice. Anyone who gets that notice has 120 days from its date to file a notarized claim with the clerk. A person other than the owner who misses that window is barred from the funds, and if no claim arrives the legal titleholder of record is presumed entitled to the money. Once the claim window closes, the clerk has 90 days to pay by priority or to file an interpleader if claims conflict. Homestead's added opening bid amount is treated as surplus and handled the same way.

Options after the April 1 delinquency

Several tools exist before a deed is ever near. Homestead owners can ask the tax collector about a deferral, filed on Form DR-570 by March 31 after the assessment year, which covers the portion of tax above a share of household income. Owners 65 or older may defer more.

  • Pay in the discount window if you can: 4 percent in November, 3 percent in December, 2 percent in January and 1 percent in February.
  • Ask the tax collector about installment prepayment, which needs an application on file by May 1 of the assessment year.
  • Call the tax collector about partial payments, which are at that office's discretion before the delinquency date.

These dates help more with next year's bill than with the one already delinquent, so mark them on a calendar.

If the owner stays after the deed sale

The deed changes who holds title, so the former owner has no right to stay once the buyer takes over. A person living in the house after the deed is in the same position as an unwanted occupant, and the buyer would use the court process or the sheriff route that fits the facts.

For an owner this is the strongest reason to act while the certificate is still outstanding. Redeeming costs the face amount plus interest and fees, and the house remains in the family. Selling to a buyer who closes quickly can pay the certificate through the title company, which treats the tax collector's payoff as one more lien to clear.

Heirs who inherit a house with a certificate on it should call the tax collector first. Ask which certificates exist, their issue dates and whether an application for a deed has been filed. The clerk can say whether a sale date is set, and the property appraiser can confirm who is listed as owner. Bring a death certificate or letters after an owner passes away, because the notice list is built from the names on record and a missed notice can affect the sale.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Costs and timing at each stage

StageTiming or amount
Taxes delinquentApril 1
Certificate soldBy June 1
RedemptionBefore deed issued; 5 percent minimum interest
Deed applicationAfter 2 years from April 1 of issuance; $75
Auction deposit5 percent or $200, balance in 24 hours
Surplus claim120 days from notice

Should you sell before a tax deed sale?

A sale ahead of the auction lets the title company pay tax and certificate charges at closing and may leave something for the owner. The payoff amount comes from the tax collector, so request it in writing before you choose a buyer.

Compare that with waiting: after a deed sale, the owner's recovery depends on a surplus that exists only if the bidding exceeds what is owed, and every lienholder is paid ahead of the former owner.

Frequently asked questions

Can an owner halt a Florida tax deed auction?

Yes, by redeeming the certificate before the deed is paid for. You pay the tax collector the face amount plus interest, costs and charges, and interest is at least 5 percent unless the certificate was bid at zero.

When can the county sale of the house happen?

The holder can apply for a deed after two years from the April 1 that falls in the year the certificate was issued. The clerk then runs the auction.

What happens if no one bids at the auction?

The land goes on the lands available for taxes list. The county has 90 days to buy it for the opening bid, and three years after the offer the land escheats to the county.

Do I get money back if the house sells high?

Possibly. A surplus is paid to lienholders first, and the titleholder is presumed entitled to what remains when no other claim arrives within 120 days. Ask the clerk about your file.

Does homestead status change the auction?

Yes. The opening bid on homestead includes one half of the latest assessed value, and small delinquencies under $250 on homestead cannot be auctioned as certificates.

Florida Real Estate Commission: What the Law Says About Agent Fees

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Real Estate Commission sale

Skip the Commission? Get a Cash Offer

Compensation questions go to the listing contract.

Selling a house in Florida?
