Who sets the commission rate?

Nobody does by statute. No Florida law fixes a commission rate for selling a home, so the fee is whatever you and the listing broker agree to in writing, and it is open to negotiation.

State law does cover the paperwork around the fee: what a listing agreement must contain, which relationships an agent may have with a client, and who may be paid for real estate services at all. Those rules are where a seller's protections sit, so skim them before you sign.

What a listing agreement must include

A real estate agent can be disciplined for a written listing agreement that leaves out any of these items:

  • a definite expiration date;
  • a description of the property;
  • the price and terms;
  • the fee or commission;
  • the signature of the principal or principals.

The broker must also hand you a legible, signed, true and correct copy within 24 hours of getting your signature. The agreement cannot make you give notice of cancellation once the listing's end date is behind you. Put simply, a Florida listing is supposed to end on the date written in it, with no automatic renewal for you to cancel.

If the listing runs out without a sale, you owe the broker nothing further unless the contract adds a tail period, so check for one before you sign. Ask for the end date in the body of the agreement, not only on a cover sheet.

Read the fee line twice. The number in your agreement governs, along with any tail period or bonus the contract adds.

Comparing listing brokers

Two brokers can quote different fees for the same house, and the fee is only part of the comparison. Lay the proposals side by side and ask about each of the following.

  • The expiration date, and whether the broker will release the listing early if the house does not sell.
  • Whether the broker will act as your single agent or as a transaction broker, in writing.
  • How and where deposits are held. Brokers must place entrusted money in escrow with a title company or bank, or in the broker's own trust account, as soon as it is received.
  • What the fee covers, and whether anything is owed if you later sell to a buyer you found yourself.

If you are also weighing an as-is cash offer, set it next to the net from a listing after the fee, repairs, carrying costs and the time the house sits on the market. Get the numbers in writing on both sides. A quick call to the closing agent for a sample settlement statement helps you see what each route leaves you with.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Can a seller avoid paying a commission?

Yes, if you hire no agent. An individual or company selling its own real property is exempt from the licensing part of the chapter, so a homeowner can sell a house without a license and without a broker's fee.

The exemption covers the owner only. It does not let you pay an unlicensed helper for finding buyers, because the law bars an agent from sharing a commission or paying other compensation to anyone who lacks the right license for referring business or doing those services. If you want help on commission, hire a broker.

There is a limit inside the exemption too. It is unavailable when a salesperson is paid strictly on a transactional basis to make sales for an owner who is in the business of selling property to the public. A homeowner with a single house sits outside that carve-out.

Agent relationships with a seller

An agent may work as a single agent or as a transaction broker, and may not act as a dual agent. Transaction brokerage is presumed unless a single-agent relationship, or no relationship, is set up in writing.

The duties differ, and the difference matters to anyone paying a commission.

Duties by type of relationship
RelationshipDuties owed to you
Single agentHonesty and fair dealing, loyalty, confidentiality, obedience, full disclosure, accounting for funds, skill and care, presenting offers, disclosing known material facts
Transaction brokerHonesty and fair dealing, accounting for funds, skill and care, presenting offers, disclosing known material facts, limited confidentiality
No brokerage relationshipHonesty and fair dealing, disclosing known material facts, accounting for entrusted funds

A single agent owes you loyalty, which a transaction broker does not. Transaction brokerage is a limited form of representation, so a seller who wants an agent pushing for the highest price should ask for single-agent status in writing.

The written disclosure

A single agent has to describe those duties in writing, either in a separate document or inside the listing agreement. The disclosure is due before or at the time you sign the listing agreement, or before the property is shown, whichever comes first.

When the notice sits inside another document, it must be in type at least as large as the rest and placed conspicuously, with the first sentence in uppercase bold. An agent who switches from single agent to transaction broker needs your written consent first.

These rules cover residential sales, meaning improved residential property of four units or fewer, unimproved land intended for four units or fewer, or agricultural property of 10 acres or fewer. Nonresidential deals, auctions and appraisals fall outside them.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

If a broker misbehaves

The same section that governs listing agreements lets the state discipline an agent for a long list of conduct. Penalties include probation, suspension for up to 10 years, revocation, a reprimand, and an administrative fine of up to $5,000 for each count or separate offense.

These grounds matter most to a home seller:

  • failing to account for or deliver money, deposits or documents that belong to someone else;
  • failing to place a deposit in escrow with a Florida title company or bank, or in the broker's own trust account, immediately on receipt;
  • fraud, misrepresentation, concealment or breach of trust in a transaction;
  • deceptive advertising of property or services;
  • giving an opinion that title is good without a current attorney's opinion, or without advising the buyer to consult an attorney or obtain title insurance.

A complaint must be filed within 5 years after the act, or within 5 years after the act was or should have been discovered with due diligence. Keep your signed listing agreement, the disclosure of the agent's duties and your closing statement for that long.

Other costs that come out of a sale

The commission is one line among several. Ask the closing agent for a written estimate of each before you list.

  • Documentary stamp tax on the deed, set at 70 cents per $100 of consideration.
  • Clerk recording charges on the deed and on any release of an old mortgage.
  • Payoff of any mortgage, liens or unpaid property taxes.
  • Prorated property taxes for the part of the year you owned the house.

A cash buyer who purchases as-is removes the agent commission line from this list, since no broker is involved, though the tax and recording items remain. Compare offers by what you would net after every line, and ask each buyer to put its terms in writing.

Frequently asked questions

Is the commission fixed by Florida law?

No. Florida statutes set no rate, so the fee comes from the listing agreement you sign and can be negotiated before signing.

Can a Florida listing agreement renew automatically?

The agreement needs a definite expiration date and cannot make you give notice to cancel after that date, so a listing should lapse on its stated date.

Do I need a license to sell my own house in Florida?

No. An owner selling their own real property is exempt from the licensing part of the chapter.

Can a Florida agent act for both buyer and seller?

No dual agency is allowed. Transaction brokerage is permitted, though it is a limited form of representation without fiduciary duties.

How soon must I get a copy of my listing agreement?

Within 24 hours. The broker must give you a signed, legible, true and correct copy within that window.

Florida Capital Gains Tax on a Home Sale: The $250,000 and $500,000 Exclusions

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Capital Gains Tax on a Home Sale sale

Selling a Florida Home? Get a Cash Offer

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

Do you owe tax on profit from selling a Florida house?

Possibly, but a federal exclusion wipes out most or all of the profit for many sellers of a main residence. A single filer can shield $250,000 of profit, and a married couple filing together can shield $500,000, provided two tests are met. The figure applies to a Florida house exactly as it would anywhere else in the country.

Florida adds local paperwork around the transfer: the deed, the stamp tax collected at recording, and the county's reassessment of the property for the next owner. Those pieces come after the federal rules below.

The two tests for the exclusion

You have to pass an ownership test and a use test within the five years ending on the closing date. Each test asks for 24 months, and the months need not be consecutive. The two tests can be met in different two-year stretches, as long as both fall inside that five-year window.

  • Ownership: title sat in your name or your spouse's for 24 of those 60 months.
  • Use: you lived in the house as your home for 24 of those 60 months. On a joint return, both spouses must pass this one.
  • Prior sale: the break is generally unavailable if you claimed it on a different house during the two years before this closing.

Publication 523, the IRS guide to selling a home, has the worksheets, the partial exclusions for early moves, and the exceptions to the two-year rule. Read it before you assume eighteen months is enough.

Figuring the taxable profit

Take the price you realize at closing and subtract your adjusted basis. Basis begins at what you paid and goes up with lasting improvements, say a new roof or a room addition. It falls with items like depreciation and insurance payments for casualty losses. Keep old closing statements and contractor receipts, because they are your proof.

Holding period decides the label. Profit on property held longer than a year is long-term and eligible for the lower rate bands. A year or less makes it short-term, taxed at ordinary wage rates. For a house that came to you by inheritance or gift, Publication 551 covers basis, which matters to a Florida family clearing out a relative's home.

A loss on a personal residence can't be deducted. Losses on investment property are different: they offset gains, and up to $3,000 of any excess ($1,500 for married filing separately) reduces other income each year, with the balance carried forward.

Federal rates on profit above the exclusion

Most net long-term gain lands in a 0%, 15% or 20% band set by taxable income, with different bands for each filing status. The bands below are for tax years beginning in 2025. Thresholds move every year, so check the IRS page for the year of your closing.

Long-term gain bands for tax years beginning in 2025
RateSingle filerJoint return
0%Income up to $48,350Income up to $96,700
15%$48,350 to $533,400$96,700 to $600,050
20%Income above the 15% bandIncome above the 15% band

Two extras can raise the bill. A 25% ceiling applies to the unrecaptured section 1250 slice of gain, which comes up when depreciation was claimed on a home office or rental space. Sellers with large investment income may also face a separate surtax described in IRS Topic 559.

Reporting a fully excluded sale

If the closing agent sends you a Form 1099-S, report the sale even though no tax results. If the gain is larger than your exclusion, report that too, on Form 8949 and Schedule D.

Keep a folder for the sale: the purchase closing statement, improvement receipts, the new settlement statement and any 1099-S. A tax preparer can work from those papers in minutes, and a missing receipt can leave a real improvement out of your basis.

Florida title companies normally prepare the 1099-S from the settlement statement. Before you sign, ask your closing agent whether one will be filed in your name. Sellers with a taxable gain may also owe estimated payments during the year, which Publication 505 explains.

Military sellers and installment sales

A service member, Foreign Service officer or intelligence community employee on qualified extended duty may elect to freeze the five-year clock for as long as ten years. Extended duty means more than 90 days or an open-ended assignment, at a post 50 or more miles from the home or in government quarters under orders. Many Florida owners near bases and ports fit this description.

A sale where the buyer pays across later years counts as an installment sale, and installment reporting is the default unless you opt out. The home sale exclusion still applies to the part you can exclude. Publication 537 and Form 6252 cover the mechanics.

Florida deed tax and reassessment

Florida charges seventy cents on each $100 of price in every county except Miami-Dade, where the printed charge is 60 cents plus a surtax. The surtax is skipped for a paper conveying only a single-family dwelling. The clerk takes the tax at recording, and the state can look to any party on the deed even when the contract puts the cost on one side.

  • A personal representative who deeds property under a probated will isn't taxed.
  • Exempt: a divorce deed for the marital home, or a deed between spouses of homestead land where the only consideration is a mortgage.
  • A Department advisement put a lady bird deed outside the stamp tax on the facts it described, so ask a Florida attorney before relying on that.

For the buyer, the assessment resets to full just value, ending the old Save Our Homes cap. Florida also hands residential buyers a written tax disclosure warning them not to assume your current bill will carry over. A homestead owner who plans to buy again should look at portability, which requires the new homestead to be established inside a three-year window counted from the year the old homestead was abandoned, with Form DR-501T filed alongside the DR-501 by March 1. These steps change the buyer's cost, not your gain.

Putting it together at closing

In order: confirm you pass the ownership and use tests, gather your basis papers, ask the closing agent about a 1099-S, and have the title agent quote the deed tax before you sign. A plain cash sale skips the buyer's mortgage taxes entirely, so on your side the tax questions stay on the profit and the deed.

Frequently asked questions

Does the federal exclusion work the same way for a Florida home?

Yes. The $250,000 and $500,000 limits come from federal tax law and apply to a main home anywhere in the country. Florida doesn't change the ownership and use tests, though the deed and county records follow Florida procedure.

How many months must I live in the house before selling?

Twenty-four months of residence and twenty-four months of ownership, both inside the five years ending at closing. The months can be scattered, and each test can be met in a different stretch.

Can I take the exclusion again soon after another sale?

Generally not. You usually can't if you excluded profit on another house during the two years before this closing. Publication 523 lists exceptions.

I will owe nothing. Do I still tell the IRS?

When a Form 1099-S shows up, yes. It has to be reported even if every dollar of gain is excludable, and also when part of the gain is taxable.

What counts toward my basis?

Your purchase cost plus lasting improvements, reduced by depreciation and insurance reimbursements for casualty losses. Inherited or gifted homes follow different basis rules in Publication 551.

A 1031 exchange requires you to identify replacement property within 45 days and receive it within 180 days, and only real property held for business or investment qualifies. These are IRS rules, not Florida rules.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

What a 1031 exchange means for a Florida owner

A 1031 exchange lets an investor who sells real property and buys replacement real property report the swap on Form 8824 instead of reporting a taxable sale. The rules now reach exchanges of real property only, and the property has to be held for business or investment rather than lived in as a main home. A Florida rental house, a small apartment building or vacant land held as an investment can all be the property you give up, and the replacement doesn't have to be in Florida.

The exchange itself is a federal tax matter. Florida adds its own paperwork, mainly the deed and the county clerk's recording of it, covered below. If you live in the house you're selling, the home sale exclusion is the relevant break, and it works differently.

The 45-day and 180-day deadlines

You have 45 days after you transfer the property you give up to name the replacement property in writing. You must receive it by the earlier of 180 days after that transfer or the due date, with extensions, of your tax return for that year. Both clocks start on the closing date of the sale, and weekends and holidays buy no extra time.

The written identification has to describe the replacement clearly. For real estate, a legal description, a street address or a distinguishable name such as an apartment building's name will do. The signed document must reach the person who is to transfer the replacement property to you, or another person involved in the exchange who isn't a disqualified person, before the 45th day ends. Alternatively, every party can sign one written agreement naming the property by that date.

  • Day 0: closing on the Florida property you are giving up.
  • Day 45: last day to identify replacement property in writing.
  • Day 180, or the return due date with extensions if sooner: last day to receive the replacement.

Because the return due date can cut the 180 days short, an owner who closes late in the year should ask a tax professional whether to extend the return to keep the full period.

Do you need a qualified intermediary?

In a deferred exchange, where the sale and the purchase close on different days, a qualified intermediary is the usual structure, and an exchange run through one still counts as like-kind. You never touch the sale money. The intermediary holds it and uses it to buy the replacement property.

The Form 8824 instructions warn that if you miss the timing rules because of the intermediary, the deal can fail as a deferred exchange and the gain may be taxable in the year you transferred the property. They also describe a qualified exchange accommodation arrangement for cases where the replacement is acquired first. Ask the intermediary how it protects your funds and what happens if a deadline is missed, and read the exchange agreement before you sign.

Which Florida properties qualify

Real property held for investment or business use qualifies. Personal property such as furniture or equipment no longer does, and your own home doesn't qualify as the property given up. The Form 8824 instructions have a section on property used as a home and on property used partly as a home, so a duplex where you live in one unit needs a careful split.

  • Likely to qualify: a rented single-family house, a small multifamily building, commercial space, farmland or raw land held for investment.
  • Unlikely to qualify: your main residence, a home held for quick resale as inventory, or a condo you use as a vacation home.
  • Needs advice: a property you rented out but also stayed in, since the mix of uses drives the answer.

Incidental personal property that goes with the real estate is acceptable only within a 15 percent limit of the replacement property's fair market value. Furnished rentals are worth raising with your tax adviser before you list.

Swaps with relatives or related companies

Special rules apply, and an exchange built to dodge them is treated as a sale. A related party includes your spouse, child, grandchild, parent, grandparent, brother or sister, and certain related corporations, partnerships, trusts, estates and tax-exempt organizations. The rule also reaches a swap made through an intermediary, and one made by a single-member LLC that you or a related party owned.

If you do a related-party exchange, you file Form 8824 for the year of the exchange and for the two years after it. Florida investors who hold property in family LLCs should list every owner before picking a replacement, since a related party on the other side can change the tax result.

Florida closing items that still apply

The Florida deed is taxed like any other sale deed. The documentary stamp tax on a deed is 70 cents per $100 of consideration in every county except Miami-Dade, where the printed rate is 60 cents plus a surtax that doesn't apply to a document transferring only a single-family dwelling. All parties to the document are liable for the tax, though the contract decides who pays it.

The deed is recorded with the clerk of the circuit court, and the recording fee schedule in section 28.24 of the Florida Statutes sets the page charges. A deed also has to be signed in front of two witnesses under section 689.01. The Department of Revenue's documentary stamp page lists which deeds are taxable.

Step or ruleRequirement

Property typeReal property only
Related partyFile Form 8824 for the exchange year and two years after

Ask your Florida title agent or closing attorney how the intermediary will receive funds. The exchange paperwork has to be in place before the sale closes.

A workable order of steps looks like this. Talk to a tax professional before you list. Hire the intermediary and sign the exchange agreement before closing. Close on the property you're giving up, and note the closing date, because both deadlines run from it. Put your replacement property in writing inside the first 45 days. Then close on the replacement and file Form 8824 with your return. A plain sale for cash skips all of this, and the gain is simply reported in the year of the sale, so the exchange only makes sense when you plan to buy another investment property right away.

Frequently asked questions

Can I do a 1031 exchange on my Florida home?

Not on a main residence. The rules cover real property held for business or investment, and Form 8824 treats property used as a home separately. If you lived in the house, look at the home sale exclusion and ask a tax professional about any rental period.

Can the 45-day or 180-day deadline be extended?

The 180-day period ends early if your tax return is due sooner, and extending the return keeps the full period open. Weekends and holidays add no days, so count calendar days from the closing.

Does Florida require a separate form for a 1031 exchange?

Ask the clerk or your title agent whether any county form applies. You report the exchange on federal Form 8824 with your return, and the deed and its stamp tax follow the usual Florida closing steps through the clerk of the circuit court.

Do I pay documentary stamp tax when I sell the old property?

Yes, the deed is taxable. Warranty, special warranty and quitclaim deeds are among the taxable documents, and all parties are liable even if the contract assigns the tax to one side. Ask your closing agent which party pays under your contract.

Can I buy replacement property in another state?

The rules don't tie replacement property to Florida. They speak of like-kind real property. Confirm the details of an out-of-state purchase with your intermediary.

Florida housing at a glance

Roughly 23,462,518 people share 10,789,047 housing units in Florida (July 1, 2025). Population is up 8.9 percent since April 2020. Builders pulled 178,297 permits in 2025, so new supply keeps coming, while the middle owner-reported home value sits at $359,000.

Of all homes, 67.6 percent have their owner living inside, so renters occupy about a third. Most people stay where they are: 86.3 percent of residents aged one and older lived at the same address a year earlier. A seller therefore finds buyers among new arrivals as often as among neighbors moving up.

People 65 and older are 22.8 percent of the population, and many hold homestead benefits that change what a buyer or heir pays after a sale.

Monthly housing costs

Owners with a mortgage spend a median $1,959 a month, and owners with no mortgage spend $673. Renters pay $1,669 in median gross rent. Each number is from the 2020 to 2024 estimates.

Subtract the second owner number from the first and you see what the loan itself adds. A paid-off house still costs money for taxes, insurance and upkeep. An heir holding a free-and-clear property pays less each month but faces vacancy risk, repairs and the autumn tax bill.

Housing situationMedian figure, 2020-2024
Home value (owners' own estimate)$359,000
Renting a home$1,669
Owning with a loan$1,959
Owning outright$673

A median of owners' estimates differs from any recorded sale price.

Transfer tax and recording charges

A deed in Florida triggers a state levy, documentary stamp tax. Seventy cents per $100 of price is the rate nearly everywhere. Miami-Dade charges 60 cents instead and layers on a 45 cent surtax, though a transfer involving only a single-family home escapes the surtax. Your contract can assign the bill to the buyer, yet each party to the document stays liable.

Then there is recording. Under s. 28.24(13) the clerk collects $5.00 on the first page and $4.00 on each additional one, along with a modernization fund charge and a $4 per page technology fee.

The tax bill has its own schedule, covered in the timeline below.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Florida house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Homestead protection and the buyer gap

Under Save Our Homes a homestead's assessed value may rise by 3 percent or CPI, whichever is smaller, until a sale sends the parcel back to just value on the next January 1. Without homestead the yearly limit is 10 percent. Two next-door houses can therefore carry very different bills.

  • Read the appraiser's record for assessed and just value.
  • Ask the tax collector about any deferral or installment plan.
  • Check that an owner who moved out has not left a stale exemption behind.

A statewide median hides all of this, so local records beat averages when you are pricing.

County offices a seller deals with

Voters in each of Florida's 67 counties choose five officers for four year terms: sheriff, supervisor of elections, and the three below, which are the ones a home seller meets.

  • Property appraiser. Values the parcel each January, sends the August notice, rules on exemption claims.
  • Tax collector. Mails bills, takes payments, processes deferral and installment requests, auctions certificates on unpaid bills.
  • Clerk of the circuit court. Files your deed, takes the stamp tax, runs foreclosure and tax deed sales.

Calling the right office first saves days at closing.

Unpaid property tax

An unpaid bill is delinquent from April 1. The tax collector then auctions a certificate on it by June 1, and bidders drive the interest rate lower in quarter percent steps. If nobody bids, the county takes the certificate at the maximum rate (s. 197.432).

The holder has to wait two years from April 1 of the issue year before asking you for payment, and that same wait applies before a tax deed application. Planning a fast sale? Settle any delinquency before you list. Lenders insist on it, and so will a cash buyer's title company.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Florida houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Use local numbers, not the state median

A single statewide median mixes beach condos, inland ranch homes and rural parcels, so it cannot price your house. Start with your county, then your neighborhood, then the house itself.

County offices hold the facts that set closing costs. The appraiser publishes values, the clerk records deeds and collects stamp tax, and the tax collector sends bills. Sale price, days on market and sales volume are not in any of those statewide averages. A local agent or the clerk's recorded sales can fill that gap.

Questions to ask each office

Write your questions down before you call, because each office answers only its own slice.

  • Appraiser: what are the current assessed and just values, and is every exemption still active?
  • Tax collector: are any taxes, deferrals or installment plans open against the parcel?
  • Clerk: how will the deed be recorded, and what stamp tax and recording charges will apply?

Answers vary by county, and a house in a high-growth county may be assessed very differently from a similar one inland. Treat the statewide figures above as background, then swap in county and city numbers when you set a price or plan repairs.

Closing agents can estimate settlement figures once they see the contract. Ask for a draft statement early rather than the week of closing.

Reading the numbers as a seller

Statewide figures tell you how the market feels, not what your house will bring. A $359,000 median sits beside a $74,568 median household income, so many buyers stretch to qualify, and that pushes some of them toward financing contingencies that cash buyers do not need. Renters paying $1,669 a month may decide ownership is within reach, but only if the carrying costs of an owned home stay predictable.

For that reason the tax side of the sale deserves early attention. A buyer will look at the recent bill and then ask what it becomes after reassessment. If your homestead cap has held your bill low for years, say so plainly in the listing conversation, and let the buyer's agent run the new numbers.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Timeline for a typical tax year

January 1 fixes assessed value and homestead status. March 1 is the filing cutoff for exemptions. The August notice shows proposed taxes and starts the petition window. Bills arrive in November with the 4 percent discount, which falls each month until February. April 1 is the delinquency date, and certificates go to auction by June 1.

Sellers who list in spring or summer are selling inside a tax year whose value was set the previous January. Plan the proration with that in mind.

From contract to closing

A contract comes first. The title company then combs the public record for liens, unpaid taxes and any other person whose signature the deed needs. You sign at the table, the clerk files the deed afterward, and stamp tax is paid on it. Your contract decides how the November tax bill gets divided.

Before you list, collect the latest bill, your exemption record and any deferral or installment papers. A surprise in one of them can add days. With a cash buyer there is no lender appraisal or underwriting, so the title search and any tax payoff set the pace.

As soon as the contract is signed, ask the closing agent for a draft settlement statement. Match each line to the office behind it: clerk, tax collector or state.

What share of Florida homes are owner-occupied?

Owners occupy 67.6 percent of homes in the 2020 to 2024 data. Households number 8,752,810 and average 2.51 people.

What does a Florida renter pay?

Median gross rent is $1,669 in the 2020 to 2024 data. Owners with a mortgage pay a median $1,959 monthly, against $673 for owners without one.

How many homes does Florida have?

The count was 10,789,047 housing units as of July 1, 2025, with an estimated 23,462,518 people living in the state.

Do Florida sellers face a deed tax?

Yes. Documentary stamp tax is 70 cents for each $100 of consideration in most counties. Miami-Dade charges 60 cents and adds a 45 cent surtax, which a transfer of only a single-family home avoids. Every party to the document is liable.

Florida Property Records: Official Records, Recording and Fees

Cash Home Buyers in Florida
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Florida Property Records: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Property Records sale
  • Turn the Florida Property Records offer down and you owe us nothing

Need Records for a Sale? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is and a title company searches the records at closing.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

Where deeds and mortgages are filed

Florida's 67 counties each keep separate Official Records under the county clerk. Whatever is filed there, whether a deed, a mortgage or a lien, can be searched by the public. The clerk also takes the deed stamp tax at the counter.

No statewide index exists. Search the Official Records of the county where the parcel sits, then turn to the property appraiser's website for the owner name, parcel number and assessed value.

Why filing a deed matters to a buyer

An unfiled deed leaves the buyer exposed. Under section 695.01, a conveyance, transfer or mortgage of real property, or a lease running a year or more, has no effect against creditors and later good-faith purchasers without notice unless it is filed as the law requires.

The same section treats a quitclaim grantee as a purchaser without notice under the recording acts. A lien from a government or quasi-government body for an improvement, service, fine or penalty binds later purchasers only when recorded. Tax, special assessment and utility liens are carved out.

Agents are covered too. A deed or mortgage signed under a power of attorney is not effective against creditors or later purchasers unless the power of attorney was recorded before their rights arose. If you are selling for an owner who cannot sign, record the power of attorney first.

Formatting rules the clerk checks

Layout rules in section 695.26 are strict enough that a nonconforming deed may be refused at the recording desk. That can push back a closing by days.

  • Every signer's name typed or printed under the signature, with a mailing address.
  • Who prepared the paper, with a mailing address.
  • Printed names and addresses for each witness.
  • A printed name under any notary's signature.
  • Blank margin boxes at the top right: 3 by 3 inches on page one, 1 by 3 inches on later pages.
  • Each grantee's name and mailing address, except on a mortgage.

Exempt from these rules: wills, plats, court orders, papers signed by public officers, instruments dated before July 1, 1991 and instruments signed outside Florida. A page the clerk accepts despite a defect stays recorded.

Witnesses on a Florida deed

Florida wants two people watching the signature. A written conveyance of a freehold, or of a term longer than one year, needs two subscribing witnesses (s. 689.01). Nobody needs a seal, and the witnessing can be done by audio-video link.

Quitclaim and lady bird deeds fall under the same rule. Leave a witness out and a title insurer may balk later.

Clerk recording fees

A closing statement shows two kinds of charge: the clerk's page fees and stamp tax. The page fees come from s. 28.24.

Clerk charges in s. 28.24 for instruments up to 14 by 8.5 inches

Records modernization trust fund$1.00 page one, $0.50 per added page
Technology add-on$4 per page
Tax deed application handling$60.00

Page count and the number of names drive the total. Call the clerk's recording desk for a figure on your actual document.

Stamp tax on a deed

Documentary stamp tax on a deed runs 70 cents per $100 of consideration (s. 201.02(1)(a)). Consideration is broad: cash, a released obligation, and any mortgage or encumbrance on the land, assumed or not.

Miami-Dade works differently, at 60 cents per $100 with a 45 cents per $100 surtax that falls away for paper moving only a single-family home. Everywhere else the 70 cents applies per $100 or portion thereof.

  • Each party to the paper is liable, even when the contract assigns payment to one side.
  • Taxable paper that never gets recorded is reported to the state revenue agency.
  • Taxable deed types: warranty, special warranty, quit claim, trustee's, life estate, contract for deed, deed in lieu, certificate of title.
  • A mortgage or note pays 35 cents per $100 secured, capped at $2,450 for the note tax.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Transfers taxed differently

Some paper escapes the tax. Under a probated will, the fiduciary's deed is not taxable. Section 201.02(7) exempts a spousal homestead deed whose only consideration is a mortgage, along with a divorce deed for the marital home.

Estate planning earns no exemption by that label alone. In advisement TAA 20B4-004 (October 2020), a lady bird deed on its particular facts moved no present beneficial interest and so owed nothing, but different facts could produce a different answer.

Separately, nearly any title transfer is a change of ownership for Save Our Homes, and the next January 1 assessment goes back to just value. Before deeding a long-held homestead, talk to the property appraiser.

Which county office holds what

A parcel's paper trail is split among three elected offices. The clerk holds recorded instruments and takes deed stamp tax, the property appraiser sets just value each January 1 and rules on exemptions, and the tax collector bills and collects.

  • Clerk: deeds, mortgages, liens, tax deed and foreclosure sale paperwork.
  • Property appraiser: ownership on the roll, TRIM notice and exemption decisions.
  • Tax collector: November bills, delinquency, tax certificates.

Plat filings carry their own clerk charge in s. 28.24: $30.00 for the first page and $15.00 for each additional page. A surveyor or developer subdividing land should budget for that separately from deed recording.

Preparing a deed so it records the first time

Most rejections are about small things. Print each signer's name beneath the signature, add the preparer's name and mailing address, and give every witness a printed name and address. Leave the top right margin blank. Name each grantee with a mailing address, unless the paper is a mortgage.

Check the number of pages and names before you go to the recording desk, since both change the fee. If the sale is by an agent for an owner, make sure the recorded power of attorney is already in the file. A deed that records cleanly the first time saves a trip and keeps the closing date where it is.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Foreclosure and tax deed sales on the record

Mortgages and liens appear in a title search and need a payoff or release before a clean deed can pass. A foreclosure sale ends in a certificate of title, on which tax is figured from the highest and best bid under s. 201.02(9).

A tax deed buyer owes stamp tax and recording fees within 24 hours of the auction, excluding weekends and holidays. A recorded contract-for-deed vendee is among the parties the tax collector notifies before that sale, which shows how recording protects an installment buyer.

Reviewing the records before you list

Order copies of the vesting deed, every recorded mortgage and any lien. They show what has to be paid at closing and whether the name on title is the name of the person who will sign.

When you got the house through an estate, a gift or an unusual deed, check with the recording desk about what it will take before picking a closing date.

Watch for government liens imposed for a fine or penalty. Section 695.01(3) makes them valid against later buyers only when a notice of lien was recorded naming the owner of record, a description or address, and the parcel number. If one sits on your parcel, study it carefully before signing a listing agreement.

Even with cash buyers there is no lender timeline to wait on, yet the title search still runs the same way. The records you pull now are what set the closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Which office takes deeds for recording in Florida?

Go to the clerk serving the land's county. Stamp tax is paid at that same counter, which is why the deed has to meet the form rules first.

What changes the recording bill?

Page count and the number of names. The first page costs more than later ones, names beyond the fourth add a charge, and trust fund and technology fees ride on top (s. 28.24(13)). The clerk will quote a total.

Is the stamp rate identical in all 67 counties?

Almost. Miami-Dade works from a separate formula, 60 cents per $100 plus a surtax of 45 cents that single-family transfers escape. Elsewhere it is 70 cents per $100.

Is an unfiled deed worthless?

Not between the signers. Section 695.01, though, strips its effect against creditors and later buyers for value who lack notice. Stamp tax applies to a deed whether or not it gets recorded.

Do the layout rules reach every instrument?

No. Wills, plats, court orders, papers signed by public officers and instruments signed outside Florida are exempt. A clerk may also take a page with odd name placement when it is clear who signed.

Selling a Rented House in Florida: Landlord and Tenant Rules

Cash Home Buyers in Florida

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Selling a Rented House in Florida sale

Selling a Tenant-Occupied House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

When a Florida rental property is sold, all security deposits and advance rents held for tenants must be transferred to the new owner or the buyer must be told to assume them. A landlord cannot use self-help to remove a tenant.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

Tenant money when you sell a rented house

Section 83.49(7) requires the seller to hand every security deposit and advance rent to the new owner, along with earned interest and an accurate accounting for each tenant. This is the landlord's job at the time of sale, so put it on the closing checklist.

Once the money and records move and the new owner or agent signs a written receipt, the seller no longer has to hold it. A new owner is presumed to have received the deposit from the previous owner, but that presumption stops at one month's rent. A buyer who never gets the transfer can face a refund claim from a tenant for money it never saw.

Deposits have their own rules while you hold them. Keep the money in a Florida account for the tenant's benefit, or post a surety bond with the circuit court clerk, and give written notice of how it is held within 30 days of receiving it. Landlords renting fewer than five units are excused from the notice, though not from holding the funds properly.

Move-out timing matters too. A landlord making no claim refunds the deposit inside 15 days of the tenancy's end. One who wants to keep part sends a written claim by certified mail or e-mail inside 30 days, and the tenant has 15 days to object. A buyer who inherits a tenancy inherits these clocks, so ask the seller for the full ledger.

  • Each tenant's deposit and advance rent amount.
  • Where the money is held and any interest earned.
  • The date each lease began and any renewal, since a renewal counts as a new rental agreement and carries the deposit forward as new.
  • A copy of each signed lease and the written notice that told the tenant how the deposit is held.
  • The name and mailing address of whoever will take over notices and rent after closing.

Can you empty the house for a sale?

Only through the notices and court steps in Chapter 83. The statute does not treat a planned sale as a reason to end a lease early, so read the lease term first and match it to the right notice period.

Section 83.57 sets the notice for ending a periodic tenancy, measured before the end of the rental period.

  • Monthly tenancy: 30 days or more.
  • Yearly tenancy: 60 days or more.
  • Quarterly tenancy: 30 days or more.
  • Weekly tenancy: 7 days or more.

A tenant with a fixed-term lease generally stays through the term unless the lease or the statute gives a ground to end it. Have a Florida landlord-tenant attorney read the lease before you tell any buyer the keys will come empty.

Notices for unpaid rent or lease violations

Nonpayment gets a 3-day notice under section 83.56(3), counted without Saturdays, Sundays or court-observed holidays. It demands the rent or possession.

Other violations fall into two kinds. For a curable violation, the tenant has 7 days after delivery to fix it. For an incurable one, such as intentional damage or continued unreasonable disturbance, the notice gives 7 days to vacate. A repeat of the same violation within 12 months lets the landlord sue without new notice.

Delivery can be by mail, by handing over a true copy, by e-mail under section 83.505, or by leaving a copy at the residence when the tenant is absent. A lease cannot waive these notice rules. If the landlord accepts partial rent after serving a 3-day notice, the landlord must give a receipt with the balance due, pay that rent into the court registry when filing, or serve a new notice.

What happens in court

The landlord files suit, the tenant gets a short window to pay rent into the registry, and a sheriff carries out any judgment.

Under section 83.60(2), a tenant who raises any defense other than payment must pay accrued rent into the court registry, or file a motion to determine rent, within 5 days after service, again excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays. A tenant who skips that step waives the defenses, and the landlord gets an immediate default judgment.

After judgment the clerk issues a writ to the sheriff, who restores possession to the landlord after 24 hours' conspicuously posted notice. Under section 83.62, weekends and holidays do not stop that 24-hour clock. Each of these steps adds days, so build your listing timeline around them.

Telling the tenant who the new landlord is

Chapter 83 has the landlord identify, in writing and by the first day of the tenancy, who the landlord or authorized notice recipient is, with a street address. Under section 83.50 that person keeps the authority until the tenant is told otherwise.

After a sale, tenants need to know where to send rent and notices. Have the closing attorney draft a written notice naming the new owner or agent, delivered to the tenant's residence or by e-mail under section 83.505.

Taxes and costs for a landlord-seller

A landlord-seller pays the same deed tax as any seller, and rental status changes how the property tax bill behaves. Section 201.02 sets deed tax at 70 cents per $100, collected by the clerk when the deed is recorded.

Rental property has no homestead protection, so the cap on a primary home does not help it. Its assessed value can rise no more than 10 percent a year, and the buyer starts at just value after the transfer. The tax collector mails bills in November, and early-payment discounts shrink each month through February.

A house that was once the owner's home and is now rented has lost its exemption, because renting ends homestead. Ask the county property appraiser to confirm the roll, and ask the tax collector for the payoff figure before closing day. A buyer's lender will want that number early.

Checklist for closing with tenants in place

Before the contract is signed, collect every lease, the deposit ledger, and proof of where the money sits. Decide whether the buyer takes the tenants or needs the house empty, and say so in the listing. If the buyer takes the tenants, the deposit transfer and the written notice about the new owner or agent belong in the closing packet.

A cash buyer can close without waiting for a lender's appraisal, which helps when a lease has only weeks left. It does not change the tenant's rights, though, so the notice periods above still control any plan to deliver the house vacant.

Frequently asked questions

What happens to my tenant's security deposit when I sell?

Pass it on. Section 83.49(7) requires the seller to give the new owner the deposits and advance rents, with earned interest and an accounting for each tenant. Once you get a written receipt, you are released from holding the money.

What notice ends a monthly tenancy?

Thirty days or more before a monthly period ends, under section 83.57. Yearly tenancies need 60 days, quarterly 30 days and weekly 7 days.

Can I evict a tenant just because I am selling?

Not on that ground alone. You need a legal basis in Chapter 83, such as a properly served nonpayment or violation notice, or the end of a periodic tenancy. Have a Florida attorney check your lease term.

How long does the 3-day notice for unpaid rent last?

Three days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays or court-observed legal holidays (section 83.56(3)). It demands payment or possession and can be delivered by mail, by hand, by e-mail, or by posting at the home if the tenant is absent.

Who tells the tenant where to send rent after a sale?

The landlord, or the person authorized to receive notices, must tell the tenant in writing. That authority stays in place under section 83.50 until the tenant hears otherwise, so a new-owner letter belongs in the closing packet.

Florida Mechanic's Lien on a Home: Deadlines and Selling With a Lien

Cash Home Buyers in Florida
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Florida Mechanic's Lien on a Home: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Mechanic's Lien on a Home sale
  • Turn the Florida Mechanic's Lien on a Home offer down and you owe us nothing

Contractor Lien on Your House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is, including houses with recorded liens.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

A Florida construction lien does not continue longer than 1 year after the claim of lien is recorded unless suit is filed, and a claim must be recorded within 90 days after the lienor's final furnishing. An owner can shorten the time with a Notice of Contest of Lien.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

What a mechanic's lien is

A mechanic's lien is a claim against a property by someone who supplied labor, services or materials and went unpaid. Florida calls it a construction lien, and Chapter 713 of the Florida Statutes says who can file one and how.

The lien attaches to the real property, not only to the contractor, so it turns up in a title search the moment the owner tries to sell. Even a subcontractor, supplier or sub-subcontractor with no contract with the owner can claim against the home under section 713.06, as long as the notice steps were followed. All liens for work under one direct contract together cannot exceed the contract price, with limited exceptions.

Deadlines for a construction lien

A claim of lien must be recorded within 90 days after the lienor's final furnishing of labor, services or materials (s. 713.08(5)). It goes to the clerk's office, and to each county if the property spans more than one.

A lienor with no direct contract with the owner has an earlier step. Section 713.06(2)(a) calls for a notice to owner before starting, or within 45 days after starting, and in any case before the owner's final payment following the contractor's affidavit. Missing that notice, or serving it late, is a complete defense to enforcement. Laborers do not need to serve it.

  • Notice to owner: before starting or within 45 days after starting.
  • Claim of lien recorded: within 90 days after final furnishing.
  • Claim of lien served on the owner: before recording or within 15 days after, or the claim is voidable to the extent the delay prejudiced someone.
  • Suit to enforce: within 1 year of recording the claim.

What a recorded claim must contain

Section 713.08 has the lienor state its name and service address, who it contracted with, the labor or materials and their price or value, a legal description, the owner's name, the first and last dates of work, and the amount unpaid.

The claim must be signed and sworn, and it must carry a statutory warning that the lien may stay valid for one year from recording and then expire unless legal proceedings have begun. An error does not automatically void it. A court can still enforce the lien against someone who was not harmed by an omission or mistake, and the claim can be amended while the recording period is open. Have a Florida attorney compare the recorded claim to this list, since defects are a common basis for contesting a lien.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How long a lien lasts and how an owner can shorten it

A lien ends one year after the claim is recorded unless an action to enforce it has begun in court within that time (s. 713.22). A recorded amended claim showing a later final furnishing date restarts the year.

The owner or the owner's attorney can shorten the wait by recording a Notice of Contest of Lien. The lienor then has 60 days from service of the notice to sue, and the lien is extinguished automatically if it does not. The clerk serves the notice on the lienor at the address in the claim and records it, and charges fees for both.

A lien that survives the year because a suit was filed is still not enforceable against creditors or later purchasers for value without notice unless a lis pendens is recorded. That is one reason title companies check the court docket as well as the property records.

Removing a lien so the house can sell

Section 713.21 lists five ways: a satisfaction entered in the clerk's record, a signed and recorded release, the lienor's failure to sue in time, a court order after a show-cause hearing, or a recorded final judgment.

  1. Pay the lienor and record a notarized satisfaction or release citing the official records reference number and recording date of the lien.
  2. Wait out the one-year period if no suit was filed, or shorten it with a Notice of Contest.
  3. File a complaint in circuit court. The clerk issues a summons telling the lienor to show cause within 20 days why the lien should not be enforced by action or canceled.
  4. Record a certified judgment showing the final outcome of any enforcement case.

A closing agent can often pay a lien from sale proceeds if the lienor supplies a payoff figure and a release. Recording the release costs clerk fees under section 28.24: $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each added page, plus the trust fund and technology charges listed there.

Lien priority against a mortgage

Recording dates decide priority. Under section 713.07, a direct contractor's lien attaches, and takes priority, as of the time the notice of commencement is recorded, or the claim of lien if no notice was recorded.

Anything recorded before that date, whether a conveyance, encumbrance or demand, ranks ahead of the lien, along with its proceeds whenever disbursed. Liens of those without a direct contract attach at recording of the claim (ss. 713.03, 713.04). So a mortgage recorded before the notice of commencement generally stands first, and one recorded afterward may not.

Avoiding double payment

Ask for a written release each time you pay the contractor, and hold the final payment until the contractor's final payment affidavit arrives. The statutory notice to owner itself warns that unpaid suppliers may lien the property even when the owner paid the contractor in full.

Under section 713.06(3)(d), the contractor gives the owner a sworn affidavit listing any unpaid lienors, and the owner keeps the final payment until it is delivered. The contractor must deliver it at least 5 days before suing to enforce a lien. An owner who fails to withhold can remain liable for valid liens the owner knows about.

Selling with a lien on the record

Ask the title company early what it sees on the record, so a lien does not surface a few days before closing. Then contact the lienor for a payoff figure and a recordable release. If the lien is disputed, a Notice of Contest or a show-cause complaint can clear it, but each takes time, so build that into the closing date.

A cash buyer does not need a lender's approval, but the buyer's title company still wants the lien paid, released or otherwise cleared at closing. Paying it from your proceeds at the table is the most common fix. Keep copies of the satisfaction and the recording receipt for your files.

Frequently asked questions

How long do I have to record a mechanic's lien in Florida?

The claim must be recorded within 90 days after final furnishing of labor, services or materials (s. 713.08(5)). A lienor with no direct contract with the owner must also serve a notice to owner on time, or the lien can be defeated.

How long does a Florida construction lien last?

One year after the claim is recorded, unless an enforcement suit begins in that time. Section 713.22 also lets an owner record a Notice of Contest that gives the lienor 60 days to sue or lose the lien.

Can I sell my house with a mechanic's lien on it?

Sometimes, but the buyer's title company will want the lien paid, released or otherwise cleared at closing. Ask the lienor for a payoff and a recordable release, or use one of the discharge methods in section 713.21.

Does the lienor have to tell me it filed a lien?

Yes. The claim of lien must be served on the owner. Under section 713.08(4)(c), failing to serve it before recording or within 15 days after makes it voidable to the extent the delay prejudiced someone.

What is a notice of commencement?

It is the owner's recorded notice for a construction project. Under section 713.07, a direct contractor's lien takes priority as of its recording, or as of the claim of lien if no notice was recorded.

content:
Selling a Florida Condo or HOA Home: Estoppel Certificates and Reserves

Cash Home Buyers in Florida
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Selling a Florida Condo or HOA Home: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Selling a Florida Condo or HOA Home sale
  • Turn the Selling a Florida Condo or HOA Home offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Condo? Get a Cash Offer

We buy condos and HOA homes as-is. Tell us about the building.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

A Florida condominium association must issue an estoppel certificate within 10 business days of a request, and the fee may not exceed $250 if nothing is owed. A buyer is jointly liable with the previous owner for unpaid assessments that came due before transfer.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

The estoppel certificate

An estoppel certificate is the association's written statement of what you owe and which fees apply to your unit or lot as of a given date. The buyer's lender and the title agent use it to set the payoff at closing. Condominium associations issue it under section 718.116(8) of the Florida Statutes, and homeowners' associations under section 720.30851.

Request it as soon as you have a signed contract. Every association has to name on its website a person or entity, with a street or email address, to receive requests, so start there.

How fast the association must deliver it

The deadline is 10 business days after the association receives a written or electronic request from the owner, the owner's designee, or the mortgagee. It goes out by hand, regular mail or email on the day it's issued. An association that misses the 10 business days can't charge a fee for that certificate.

A summary court proceeding under section 51.011 can compel compliance, and the winning side recovers reasonable attorney fees. Most sellers never need it, but it shows how seriously the statute treats the deadline.

  • Effective period: 30 days if hand delivered or emailed, 35 days if sent by regular mail.
  • Amended certificate: free if new information or a mistake turns up in that period, and it starts a new 30 or 35 days.
  • Reliance: the association gives up the right to collect more than the stated amounts from anyone who relies on the certificate in good faith.

Estoppel fees

The fee is capped at $250 when no delinquent amounts are owed on the unit. A request delivered within 3 business days on an expedited basis may add $100. If money is owed to the association, the added fee can't exceed $150. Fee authority has to come from a written board resolution or a written management contract.

The caps adjust every five years by the Consumer Price Index, and the Department of Business and Professional Regulation posts the adjusted amounts on its website, so check there before you pay. If the closing falls through and a payer who isn't the owner asks within 30 days after the closing date, the fee is refunded within 30 days of the request, and the owner is responsible for the refund.

Estoppel certificate fee limits, sections 718.116 and 720.30851

No delinquencyReasonable fee, not over $250
Expedited, within 3 business daysAdditional $100
Delinquent amount owedAdditional fee not over $150
Late delivery past 10 business daysNo fee
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What the certificate lists

It shows the regular assessment and how often it's paid, the date it's paid through, and the next installment due. It also carries an itemized list of all assessments, special assessments and other money owed, plus items scheduled to come due during the effective period.

The form asks other questions worth answering for yourself before the buyer sees them.

  • Is a capital contribution, resale or transfer fee due, and how much?
  • Is any rule violation open and noticed to the owner?
  • Does the board need to approve the transfer, and has it?
  • Is there a right of first refusal for members or the association, and has it been exercised?
  • Which other associations is the unit a member of, and who insures the association?

The condominium form adds a line for a parking or garage space number and, where the account went to collections, the name and contact information of the attorney. The association can't charge for that line.

Do unpaid assessments follow the unit to the buyer?

To a degree, yes. Under section 718.116(1), a new unit owner is jointly and severally liable with the previous owner for unpaid assessments that came due before transfer. The new owner may recover from the seller, and whoever acquires title must pay the association within 30 days after the transfer.

Unpaid assessments bear interest at the declaration's rate, or 18 percent a year if the declaration names none. If the declaration allows it, the association may add a late fee of up to the greater of $25 or 5 percent of the late installment. Payments are applied first to interest, then late fees, then collection costs and attorney fees, then the assessment itself.

An association also holds a lien on the condominium parcel. A claim of lien stops being effective one year after recording unless the association starts a suit, and an owner can record a notice of contest that gives the association 90 days to sue. Pay the estoppel figure at closing so the title agent can obtain a lien release.

Documents a condo seller hands the buyer

At the seller's expense, the buyer is entitled to a current copy of the declaration, the articles of incorporation, the bylaws and rules, the annual financial statement and budget, and the Frequently Asked Questions and Answers document. Section 718.503(2) also lists the inspector-prepared summary of any milestone inspection report and the most recent structural integrity reserve study, or a statement that none has been completed.

A resale contract must carry one of two clauses in conspicuous type. One says the buyer received the documents more than 7 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, before signing. The other makes the agreement voidable by written notice within 7 such days after signing and receipt of the documents. A contract missing the required wording can be voided by the buyer before closing.

Reserves and structural studies

A buyer and the buyer's lender will read the budget. Under section 718.112 it must include reserve accounts for roof replacement, building painting, pavement resurfacing and any other item whose deferred maintenance or replacement cost exceeds $25,000, or the inflation-adjusted amount published by the division if greater. The amount is worked out from estimated remaining useful life and replacement cost.

Residential condominium associations must also complete a structural integrity reserve study at least every 10 years for each building of three habitable stories or higher. Ask the association whether its study is on file, since the buyer must receive it or a statement that none exists.

The same section lists buildings the study rule doesn't reach, including those under three stories and one- to four-family dwellings with three or fewer habitable stories. A seller in a low-rise community should check the declaration to see which rules apply.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an association have to issue an estoppel certificate?

Ten business days after a written or electronic request from the owner, the owner's designee or the mortgagee. If it's late, the association can't charge for it. Condominium and homeowners' association statutes use the same period.

What is the most an association can charge for the certificate?

The cap is $250 when no money is owed, with $100 more for delivery within 3 business days and up to $150 more when an amount is delinquent. The caps adjust every five years, so check the Department of Business and Professional Regulation website for current figures.

How long is an estoppel certificate good for?

Thirty days if hand delivered or sent electronically, and 35 days if mailed. If the sale or refinance hasn't closed in that window, ask for an amended certificate, which carries no fee and starts a new period.

Do I owe condo assessments after I sell?

You owe the assessments that came due while you owned the unit. The new owner shares liability for unpaid assessments through the transfer date, but the buyer may recover from you, so pay the estoppel balance at closing.

Does a Florida condo seller have to give the buyer a reserve study?

Yes, where one exists. Section 718.503 entitles the buyer to the most recent structural integrity reserve study or a statement that none has been completed, along with the budget and governing documents, at the seller's expense.

Florida Reverse Mortgage: Selling or Inheriting a Home With a HECM

Cash Home Buyers in Florida
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Florida Reverse Mortgage: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Reverse Mortgage sale
  • Turn the Florida Reverse Mortgage offer down and you owe us nothing

Inherited a Home With a Reverse Mortgage? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is and work with the lender and title company.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

When the borrower dies

The loan balance becomes due and payable. The loan must be satisfied by the thirtieth day after the borrower dies, though the lender may approve 90-day extensions if the estate or heirs show they are actively trying to sell or repay.

A HECM, or Home Equity Conversion Mortgage, is the reverse mortgage insured by the Federal Housing Administration. While the borrower lives in the house, no payments are due. The balance comes due when the borrower sells, stops using the home as a main home, or dies as the last surviving borrower. No more funds can be paid out once that point is reached.

Those 30 days run out long before most Florida probate cases finish. Call the loan servicer first, ahead of any court filing.

How a HECM works during the borrower's life

The HECM is the only reverse mortgage insured by the federal government, and it comes through an FHA-approved lender. Borrowers can live in the home indefinitely as long as property taxes and homeowner's insurance stay current.

The amount a borrower can draw depends on three inputs:

  • the age of the youngest borrower or eligible non-borrowing spouse;
  • the current interest rate;
  • the lesser of the appraised value, the FHA mortgage limit or the sales price.

Heirs weighing a sale should find out whether the borrower fell behind on taxes or insurance, since that is a common reason servicers call a loan due. Free HUD counseling is available at (800) 569-4287. Never pay anyone for information that HUD gives out at no charge.

What choices Florida heirs have

Heirs other than a non-borrowing spouse can repay the loan, sell the home, or hand the property to the lender by a deed in lieu to head off foreclosure. The estate carries property taxes and insurance until title moves.

Heirs' options for a HECM home
OptionWhat happens
Sell the homeIf the balance exceeds the home's value, a sale at 95 percent or more of current appraised value lets the lender accept the net proceeds as full payment
Keep the homeThe loan balance must be paid off in full
Deed in lieuTitle goes to the lender to avoid foreclosure
Extension90-day extensions possible with proof of active efforts to sell or repay

Any transfer after the death is treated as a "sale" for the 95 percent rule.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

If the borrower's spouse still lives in the house

A spouse who never signed the loan might still be protected. Repayment can be postponed so that spouse stays in the property for life, but among other conditions the lender needs a Non-Borrowing Spouse Certification within 30 days of the last surviving borrower's death.

That 30-day clock is the one most easily missed during a funeral week. If you are a surviving spouse who was not on the loan, contact the lender and the FHA Resource Center at (800) 225-5342 before any other paperwork.

Bring the marriage certificate and some proof that the spouse lives in the home, because the lender will want support for the claim. Do not sign a sale contract or a deed until the lender confirms in writing whether the spouse's protection applies.

Whether a particular spouse qualifies depends on conditions the lender can explain, so ask for them in writing.

What heirs should line up before calling a buyer

If you have the facts in hand, a buyer, the servicer and the title company can all work from the same numbers. Gather these before accepting any offer:

  • the death certificate and the loan number;
  • the servicer's current payoff figure, requested in writing;
  • proof that taxes and insurance are current, since those costs stay with the estate;
  • a current appraisal, because the 95 percent figure is measured against appraised value;
  • the personal representative's name and, where probate is open, a copy of the letters from the court.

If the lender has granted a 90-day extension, keep the paperwork showing active efforts, such as the listing agreement or a signed purchase contract. The servicer can ask for that proof at any time.

Ask the title company early which of these items it wants in hand. A cash buyer who takes the home in its current condition can often close within the servicer's window, because there is no lender appraisal to wait on.

Heirs who disagree about selling should settle it early. The servicer's clock keeps running while relatives argue, and only a person with legal authority over the estate can sign a deed.

How Florida probate affects the sale

Title to the house is typically in the decedent's name alone, so a court-appointed person has to sign the deed. Two court routes exist. Summary administration fits when the non-exempt estate is no more than $150,000 or the death was more than two years ago. Anything else goes through formal administration. The county probate clerk can tell you which applies to your file.

Two points control the calendar:

  • Creditors lose their claims unless they file by whichever comes later: 3 months after the creditor notice is first published, or 30 days after service on a creditor who was entitled to direct notice. The reverse mortgage lender holds a secured loan, so ask the servicer what it plans to do.
  • A deed from a personal representative acting under a probated will carries no documentary stamp tax.

Florida has had no estate tax for deaths after 2004. Since July 1, 2023, personal representatives no longer file Form DR-312 or DR-313.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

If the lender starts foreclosure

A lender in Florida has to foreclose through a court. When a final judgment is entered, the clerk holds a public sale somewhere between 20 and 35 days later, unless the plaintiff agrees to wait longer. Whoever wins the bidding puts down a 5 percent deposit.

If you want to stay out of court, the deed in lieu above is the alternative. Save every servicer letter and respond to court papers on time, because a missed date narrows what is left for you to do.

Selling before judgment gives you the most room. A buyer who can close fast pays off the HECM balance at the table, and one who accepts the house in its current condition fits an estate with no money for repairs.

Property taxes and homestead

Homestead protection lasts only while the home remains the borrower's permanent residence. Renting it out, moving out for good or giving up Florida residency ends it.

After the borrower dies, any sale or title transfer is new ownership. The January 1 that follows resets assessed value to just value unless an exception fits. Meanwhile the estate keeps paying taxes and insurance until title moves, so build those into your budget.

Three calls sharpen the numbers: the lender for a payoff figure, an appraiser for current value, and the county property appraiser for the likely assessment change.

Frequently asked questions

How long do heirs have to pay off a HECM?

The loan must be satisfied in the first 30 days after the borrower's death. The lender may approve 90-day extensions with documentation of active efforts to sell or repay.

Do heirs owe more than the house is worth?

If the balance exceeds the home's value, heirs may sell for at least 95 percent of the current appraised value and the lender will accept the net proceeds as satisfaction of the loan.

Can heirs keep the house?

Yes, if the HECM balance is paid off in full. That is the condition for keeping the home.

What can a surviving spouse who was not on the loan do?

Special provisions may allow the spouse to stay for life, but a Non-Borrowing Spouse Certification is due to the lender in the first 30 days after the last borrower's death.

Who pays property taxes on the house after the borrower dies?

Property taxes and insurance remain the responsibility of the borrower's estate until title is transferred.
